papers.title: IndicTalk
papers.summary: 1,328,604 event-grounded multi-turn conversations, 18 language varieties, 9 Indic languages, code-mixed in both native-script and Romanized forms; built via news-grounding + persona-conditioned generation + automatic quality validation. Directly serves the project's stated #1 task (conversation); nothing else at this scale exists for Indic code-mixed dialogue. The paper says 'we will release' — verify the data is actually up before planning around it.

papers.title: Indic DiarBench
papers.summary: ~108 hours across all 22 scheduled languages with human-corrected, time-aligned, speaker-attributed transcriptions; near-field meetings, far-field and in-the-wild, capturing code-mixing, dialect and speaker overlap. First joint diarization+ASR benchmark covering all 22 languages. Open access — add to the EVAL suite.

papers.title: BHARATI
papers.summary: Morphology-aware SentencePiece BPE tokenizers on a 781MB balanced corpus across seven languages, handling Sanskrit/Tamil agglutination and sandhi. Achieves 2.6 tokens per Indian Knowledge System technical term vs 5.25 for GPT-2 and ~90% sequence-length reduction vs GPT-2/byte-level on a released 490-sentence IKS test set, with the measurement script published.

papers.title: The Tokenizer Tax
papers.summary: Measured on FLORES-200 across six tokenizers and fourteen Indian languages: an average 8.0x tokenization tax under cl100k_base (13.0x for Malayalam), effective context window cut to as little as 12%, mechanism identified as failed byte-pair merges (Pearson r = 0.89), and XLM-R/o200k_base reducing the average Indic tax by 73%. Quantifies and validates the main document's claim that the tokenizer decision is worth more than 2T extra tokens; elevates it from workstream to gating milestone.

papers.title: Can OCR-VLMs Read Devanagari? A Stress-Test Benchmark and Post-Correction Study
papers.summary: Ten systems benchmarked on Hindi/Devanagari across four synthetic degradations and 300 real printed scans. On clean rendered text all ten cluster at chrF++ 91-98; on real scans nine of ten collapse across a 76-point range. EasyOCR falls 93.6 -> 58.3, GPT-5.5 drops to 58.5, and olmOCR-7B falls to 40.5 — worst in class. Qwen3-VL-8B wins among open models at 75.2 on a single 24 GB GPU; DeepSeek-OCR has the best median but rare catastrophic repetition failures (up to 71x reference length). Reverses the main document's 'fine-tune olmOCR for Indic' recommendation.

papers.title: Conversational IndicTrans2 adaptation
papers.summary: Adapts IndicTrans2-1B to conversational register across all 21 Indic languages using only public data (OpenSubtitles, BPCC-H-Daily, Tatoeba) via experience replay + model souping: +6.2 mean conversational chrF with no FLORES regression. Directly reusable recipe. The authors' own blind human + multi-model check did not confirm a perceived quality improvement — they call it register matching, not better translation; the document says adopt the technique and the scepticism.

papers.title: SCRIBE
papers.summary: Diagnostic evaluation plus rich transcription models for Indic ASR. Useful for the ASR-transcription pipeline of Section 8.

papers.title: IndicKLAR
papers.summary: Cross-lingual knowledge consistency, code-mixed vs native, across nine open-weight models: the native-language accuracy gap to English reaches ~0.50, but code-mixed inputs close most of it — to within ~0.05 of English — with no model-level intervention. Strategically important: suggests code-mixed input is a far more efficient path to Indic parity than native-script-only training, and should influence the data mixture.

papers.title: AgriGov
papers.summary: Structured multilingual dataset of Indian government farmer schemes. Domain-specific; matches BharatGen's agriculture vertical.

papers.title: Darshana Graph
papers.summary: Parallel commentary corpus for comparative Indian philosophy. Rare classical/Indian Knowledge System content.

papers.title: BhashaSutra
papers.summary: Task-centric unified survey of Indian NLP datasets. The document recommends using it as the master index — 'the most complete catalogue in existence'. Date given only as 'Apr 2026' in Addendum A.4 (and as '2026' in the Section 20 source index), with no day, so the date field is null.

papers.title: DataOrchestra: Learning to Orchestrate Per-Example Curation of Pretraining Data
papers.summary: The successor research line to OPUS-style selection, but for per-example processing: an orchestrator decides drop/keep/clean per chunk, then selects operations from programmatic edits to LLM rewriting with a generated instruction per rewrite. Validated by from-scratch pretrains at 0.5B-7B with stable average gains across 11 benchmarks, and effective for math continued-pretraining. To be read before finalizing the Section 17 pipeline — it is the strongest current argument that per-example adaptivity pays at the cleaning stage rather than the selection stage.

papers.title: IKS-Instruct
papers.summary: 24,795 instruction pairs across 7 languages (en/hi/sa/ta/te/kn/ml), 41 Vedic pedagogical techniques, aligned to CBSE classes 6-12; sources include the Bhagavad Gita, Thirukkural, Sangam literature, Vedic texts, Vedic-math sutra demonstrations, bilingual pairs and multi-turn dialogues. Fills two flagged gaps: BhashaBench's weakest domain (Ayurveda, GPT-4o 59.74%) and Section 10.1's proposed syllabus-structure curriculum-generation workaround, now executed by someone else. Licence unverified — check before ingestion.

papers.title: MoLGE: Mixture of Language-Group Experts
papers.summary: Dedicated experts per cluster of similar languages plus hierarchical LoRA for massively multilingual ASR, studying linguistic vs data-driven grouping criteria. Design evidence for MoE routing: converges from the ASR side with BharatGen's observation that MoE layers spontaneously grouped Hindi/Marathi and with Param-2's shared+routed expert split. Language-group experts (not per-language) are emerging as the pattern for 22-language capacity without dilution.

papers.title: The Physics of Multi-Turn Long-Horizon Planning
papers.summary: Controlled environment isolating how planning ability is acquired across pre- and post-training. Three findings for agentic data: explicit world-model construction via chain-of-thought state-transition data in pre-training yields stronger long-horizon generalization; atomic skills alone do not compose, but a little long-horizon data works; and suboptimal trajectories severely impair performance because errors amplify over horizons — so filter agentic traces hard rather than maximizing volume.

papers.title: XIH-Bench / Language Shapes Instruction-Hierarchy Compliance
papers.summary: Six languages, same- and cross-language instruction conflicts. Names a new failure mode — the 'Language Boundary Effect', where cross-language conflicts get higher compliance than same-language — and finds that language specialization makes lower-priority instructions in model-favored languages harder to override. Threat-model translation: an Indic-expert model acquires a jailbreak surface of injections written in its own favored languages, so cross-language-injection red-teaming joins the 22-language safety plan.

papers.title: PatiGonit22K
papers.summary: 22,441 Bengali math word problems, simple through multi-operation, translated/annotated/culturally adapted/verified. Corrects the report: Section 6 said Indic math/STEM is 'essentially absent'; amend to 'nearly absent' — this exists, though four orders of magnitude below MegaMath. The generate-and-translate strategy of Section 6 stands.

papers.title: Systematic analysis of LLM and transformer MT for English-Tamil across diverse data
papers.summary: Added to the Section 7 translation evidence base. The document records no further detail and issues no strategy change on the back of it.

risks.mitigation: Per-repo containers, 100-turn rollouts, harness co-development. Start the NeMo Gym work in parallel with data, not after.

risks.mitigation: §12.3, plus a fully held-out benchmark and a private eval set.

risks.mitigation: Use shared + routed experts (Param-2 uses 64 experts with 2 shared for code-mixing/domain-mixing) and monitor per-language expert utilisation from step one.
risks.note: §18.1. BharatGen reported MoE layers naturally grouping related languages (Hindi/Marathi). §B.5 adds MoLGE (arXiv:2607.24030) as converging evidence that language-*group* experts, not per-language experts, are the emerging pattern for 22-language capacity without dilution.

risks.mitigation: Keep the ✅ clean tier separable so you can retrain a compliant base if needed. Do not architect a corpus you cannot decompose.
risks.note: §18.2. The §18.2 table has no severity column, so the document assigns no severity; the section is titled "Legal and reputational risks" without labelling rows individually as legal or reputational. §14.1: the ruling is a single-judge interim order resting on a stretched Section 52(1)(a)(i), "one appeal away from re-examination".

risks.mitigation: Provenance index from day one; document-hash→shard→checkpoint lineage.

corrections.before: §1.3 listed tokenizer fertility as one of three things that will determine whether the model is good, asserted that "your tokenizer decision is worth more than 2T extra tokens", and told you to "budget a dedicated workstream". §18.1 rated it a High technical risk with the same workstream mitigation.

corrections.before: §16 budgeted the corpus in unique tokens seen once: ~0.3T naturally-occurring Indic tokens exist, therefore natural Indic can only be ~2.0% of a 15T mix ("that ratio is uncomfortable and it is also unavoidable"), the 40–70% dedup loss is the single most likely schedule-breaker (§18.1), and the 20T milestone requires "aggressive multi-epoch reuse" left hand-waved.
corrections.after: Budget in unique pool × deliberate epoch schedule = effective tokens. ~0.3T unique natural Indic × 4 epochs ≈ 1.2T effective at roughly zero quality cost, with a theoretical ceiling of ~4.8T effective at 16× — raising the natural-Indic effective share from ~2% to ~7–8% without collecting a single new token. Two-to-four epochs on the highest-quality tiers (FineWeb-Edu, curated-clean) is cheap and standard. The dedup risk is half-defused: dedup down to the unique pool, then choose repetition deliberately, because dedup ≠ see-once. The 20T milestone becomes principled and quantified — ~11–13T unique plus a scheduled epoch plan concentrated on the scarce, high-value tiers.
corrections.why: The section-16 math was "Chinchilla-brained": it silently assumed every token is seen once. Muennighoff et al. measured that up to 4 epochs of repeated data is almost as good as fresh data — an 8.7B model trained 4 epochs on 44B unique tokens finished with only 0.5% higher validation loss than a single-epoch model on 178B unique tokens — with a decay constant R*_D ≈ 15, worthlessness at 40 epochs, a hard ceiling at U·(1+R*_D) ≈ 16× the unique pool, and an allocation rule that when data-constrained you scale epochs faster than parameters. Two honest limits attach: the measurements are English web data at ≤9B parameters, and nobody has measured R*_D for Indic, translated or synthetic text; and repetition works on whole tiers, not slivers (up-sampling 0.1% of a corpus 100× significantly degrades performance).
corrections.source: arXiv:2305.16264 — Muennighoff et al., "Scaling Data-Constrained Language Models" (in-project); arXiv:2401.00448 — Sardana & Frankle, cited at thesis level only

corrections.before: §17's pipeline treated the mixture as static and phase-scheduled (§16.3), and considered neither what a per-iteration data selector costs at scale nor what an English-trained quality classifier does to Indic data.
corrections.after: Static phase-scheduled mixing is confirmed as the production backbone — it is what the only in-project 120B run actually shipped with. Add an Always-ON lane: ~8% of every batch reserved for Tier-2/3 Indic scripts, agentic/world-model traces and benchmark training splits, bypassing every selector and quality classifier. Demote dynamic selection to ablation-stage tooling, never with an English-heavy reference proxy, and evaluate DataOrchestra for the *cleaning* stage instead of the selection stage.
corrections.why: LightningLM's golden proxy was English-heavy (cosine 0.876 with the English web band), so OPUS systematically under-valued Indic data and would have rejected it — "a single selector should not govern data whose value it cannot see". FineWeb-Edu-style quality classifiers carry exactly the same bias, so the Always-ON lane is the mechanism that guarantees Bodo, Santali, Dogri and Manipuri actually train at every stage. The economics also do not hold up: OPUS cost ~17% wall-clock throughput at the 5B stage in a sharded stack (30,429 vs 36,737 tok/s) against the 4.7% its own paper reports, and was disabled at 2B and again from 9B onward. The document marks this a 🔴 REVISION, though not one of the three labelled MATERIAL CORRECTIONs.
corrections.source: arXiv:2606.07404 — LightningLM 0.1V technical report (in-project); arXiv:2607.24717 — DataOrchestra, 28 July 2026

corrections.before: The main document framed the programme as which 300B to train from scratch — §1.2 recommends architecting for 15T tokens, and §16/§19 sequence a from-scratch run.

corrections.before: The mix engine computed effective tokens as unique pool x epochs, a plain multiplication, and chapter 2 rendered the product as the value of a repetition schedule. Its ladder ran to 20 passes over a 336B natural-Indic pool and displayed 6.72T, badged UNEVIDENCED on the grounds that "published work stops at 16". The rail said nobody had measured repetition for Indian text.
corrections.after: Seen tokens and worth tokens are now separate quantities. Seen stays linear, because that is what compute is billed on. Worth follows Muennighoff et al. (JMLR v26, 2025) Eq. 18: D' = U + 15.4.U.(1 - e^(-(passes-1)/15.4)). Four passes are worth 3.73x rather than 4x, sixteen 10.6x rather than 16x, forty 15.2x rather than 40x, and no schedule exceeds 16.4x the unique pool. The 6.72T figure was not unevidenced but unreachable: the ceiling for a 336B pool is 5.51T at any number of passes. 16 epochs is the half-life at which a repeated token has lost 1/e of its value, not the end of the evidence — the same paper reports 44-epoch runs and labels 40 epochs worthless. And ATLAS (ICLR 2026, 774 runs over MADLAD-400) fits the curve per language and finds Hindi's tail bends upward sooner than English, so the constants are the optimistic end for an Indic pool rather than the neutral one. A guardrail now errors on any schedule asking a pool for more than repetition can be worth.
corrections.why: The multiplication is correct for cost and wrong for value, and the word "effective" let a compute-side quantity stand in for a data-side claim — which is the exact shape of the "Chinchilla-brained" error this project had already corrected once in the other direction. Two of the surrounding statements were also false rather than merely optimistic. The strategic consequence is larger than the arithmetic: Kimi K2 measured ten epochs of raw repetition at ~23.8% against ~28.9% for ten rephrasings read once, and Kimi K3's pre-training section does not use the word epoch at all, rephrasing knowledge and mathematics corpora with fidelity verification instead. Re-reading is the weakest answer to a scarce pool that is still better than nothing; this page does not yet cost a rephrasing pipeline, which is the open question the correction leaves behind.
corrections.source: Muennighoff et al., Scaling Data-Constrained Language Models, JMLR v26 (2025), Eq. 18 and Fig. 1; ATLAS, ICLR 2026, arXiv:2510.22037; Kimi K2, arXiv:2507.20534; Kimi K3, arXiv:2607.24653 SS3.1; DeepSeek-V3, arXiv:2412.19437

corrections.before: The contamination gate tokenised with the regular expression `\w+`, and reported an index of 411,442 thirteen-word fingerprints over MILU's validation split, of which 56 items were too short for the full window. The page described a shingle as thirteen consecutive words and said that thirteen words agreeing by chance is not a thing that happens.
corrections.after: Tokenisation keeps Unicode combining marks and composes to NFC, so a word is a word in every script. The same corpus indexes to 126,044 fingerprints at eight window widths, and 1,090 of the 8,923 items - not 56 - are genuinely shorter than the thirteen-word window. The floor below which an item is refused rose from 5 to 6, because the example the code's own comment gives as too generic to index ("what is the capital of") is five words long. The browser demo carried the identical defect in its own tokeniser and now mirrors the pipeline, including the floor: it used to tell a reader that any question under thirteen words was unprotectable, which contradicted both the pipeline and the paragraph beneath it.
corrections.why: Python's `\w` matches letters, digits and underscore but not combining marks, and every Indic vowel sign, virama, anusvara and nukta is a combining mark. So `\w+` split every Indic word at every vowel sign and discarded the sign: five Hindi words became eleven consonant fragments. 91% of the indexed items are in Indic scripts and inflated by a mean factor of 2.58, so a "thirteen-word fingerprint" was roughly five real words of skeleton there - and the gate produced false positives that would have deleted clean training text. Measured against 203,388 held-out FLORES-200 sentences the old tokeniser collided with 5 of them, all Indic, all ordinary news prose; the corrected one collides with none. One of the five was the Malayalam for "the attack greatly affected relations between India and Pakistan" - three ordinary words that normalised to a full thirteen-token window. The loss would have been silent and would have fallen on the scarcest tier in the mixture, the one the protected lane exists to defend. The suite passed throughout: 174 tests, none of which had ever been run against text in the scripts the gate was built for.
corrections.source: Measured in this repository: dataframework/shingles.py, data/benchmarks/MILU.json (8,923 items) and data/corpora/flores200_dataset (203,388 held-out sentences)

corrections.before: The `sourcing`, `lifecycle` and `orphan_tiers` blocks each declared `provenance: "measured"` over every number inside them, including committed_tokens of 6.39T. Three figures in the browser did the same by hand, one of them a counterfactual - what the corpus would hold if the reader resolved blockers that have not been resolved. 115 fertility values claimed to be measured against a run id literally prefixed `pending-`, and `protocol_gaps` stated that three of six tokenizers were unavailable.
corrections.after: A derived number is no more measured than its least-measured input. The three blocks are estimated, because every token figure in them is a sum over the catalogue's size_tokens and not one of the 145 records carries a measured size - 24 are estimated and 121 unknown. Exact counts keep the mark they earned: sourcing.counts, record_counts and grades are still measured, because counting records in a catalogue we hold is a measurement and a miscount would be a bug rather than an estimate. The run-id substitution now walks every block instead of one, so no placeholder ships; `protocol_gaps` is computed from the run and reads 5 tokenizers measured and 1 unavailable.
corrections.why: The page tells the reader that the green underline means somebody ran it. Nobody had run the 6.39T, and the mark is worth nothing if it can be applied to a sum of estimates. The invariant that should have caught this could not: it let a `provenance` key at the top of a block cover every number beneath it at any depth, so one declaration exempted 404 numeric leaves. The fertility case was the same failure in a different shape - the guard asked only whether a source contained an "@", not whether the id it named was a real run. Four guards now check the claims rather than the shape of the claims, each watched failing before being trusted. Per-field typing of the mixed count-and-token blocks remains the deeper fix and is not done here: the blocks under-claim on their exact counts rather than over-claim on their sums, which is the safe direction of the two.
corrections.source: Measured in this repository: web/data.json, records/fertility.json, dataframework/

corrections.before: Three of the guards enforcing the five invariants could not fail. INV-1b's mutation proof built a string from an eval item and asserted the item was in it. INV-2's check asked `is_commercially_usable(grade)` inside `if grade == "X"`, and that function was `grade != "X"` - so it reduced to asserting that "X" equals "X". The leak scan looked only for synthetic fixtures that were never within reach of the pipeline. Separately, `score_gates` summed whatever keys it was handed, `coverage.py`'s exclusion clause could only ever fire for one capability, `mix.check` skipped its ceiling test in silence on a tier with no stated pool, and the page disclosed one of the two guardrails its own mixture breaches.
corrections.after: The guards test the claims rather than restating the implementations. INV-2 reads the shipped plan and asserts no grade-X id reaches a committed tier; its mutation commits one and watches the guard object. `is_commercially_usable` takes the record and requires an established licence, because unknown is not permission - which the rest of the framework says and this function contradicted. The leak scan runs the real benchmark corpus when it is present, and its proof runs the same scanner over a bundle carrying an item. `score_gates` counts only the five named gates. `coverage.py` separates a substring trap from an outright disqualifier, so the india-context exclusion runs for the first time: IndicMMLU-Pro no longer counts as an instrument for Indian worldview, because its own notes say it was translated. `mix.check` reports an unassessable tier instead of skipping it, errors on a negative schedule, and no longer raises on a null one. And the mixture's synthetic-Indic breach is stated on the page beside the protected-lane breach.
corrections.why: A guard that cannot fail is worse than no guard, because it produces the confidence of a passing suite without the fact of one. Two of the five invariants were in that state while the page told readers each ships with a test proving it fails when broken. The grading consequences were live rather than theoretical: a duplicated gate key could score 14 out of a stated maximum of 10 and buy a grade A, and a dataset with no established licence answered True to the one function INV-2 exposes. The coverage exclusion had never run at all, so a translated benchmark was being counted as evidence for the capability the model is named for. Disclosing one breach and not the other was the subtlest of these: it reads as candour while showing half the picture.
corrections.source: Measured in this repository: dataframework/, tests/, web/data.json

corrections.before: The opening paragraph called the corpus 17 trillion tokens because 16.8 was rounded to zero decimals, while every other mention said 16.8T. Chapter 4 said the mixture had eight tiers and ten tiers on one screen, beside a figure drawing ten bars. The glossary defined a rung as one of 5, 10, 15 or 20 trillion tokens - a ladder replaced by 3T/8T/16.8T/30T - and defined a pass as contributing four times the pool's size, which is the arithmetic X15 exists to retract. Chapter 13 said all four licence-blocked datasets were English corpora and planned against 35,000 hours of open Indic speech. The cost chapter priced a 15T run. Two figures were both numbered Fig. 9. Sarvam-30B was 30B in one register and 32B in another, and both cited the model cards for token counts the cards do not state.
corrections.after: Every count and figure quoted in prose is read from the record that holds it: the tier count, the ladder top, the rung set, the preference-to-demonstration ratio. The budget renders to one decimal. The glossary states that four passes cost four times the compute and are worth about 3.7 times the pool. Chapter 13 says none of the four is an Indic corpus - two are English-only, two are multilingual with unmeasured Indian partitions, which is why they cannot be budgeted against - and plans against the 100,000+ hours correction X04 established. `run_cost.py` recomputes the run from the shipping budget: 2.80M H100-hours and $5.6M, not 2.50M and $5.0M. Post-training is Fig. 7. Sarvam's counts match the model cards and the token citations point at the blog that states them. The legend says what grade A requires and that nothing reaches it, so "four are committable today" no longer reads against "A usable (0)".
corrections.why: Every one of these is the same defect: a number typed into a sentence beside data that later moved. It is the fourth time this class has been corrected here - the seed's text called a 3B model a dense 40B, the third growth stage claimed to add 80B parameters where it adds 32B, the changelog quoted the pre-X16 shingle count - so this correction fixes the cause rather than the instances: prose that quotes a count now reads it. Where a figure genuinely cannot be computed, a test asserts the two records agree. The cost record is the second derivation to be moved out of static JSON for exactly this reason, after the vocabulary trade.
corrections.source: Measured in this repository: web/data.json, records/, web/chapters.js

corrections.before: A grade was a score and nothing else. UNKNOWN and FAIL both contributed 0, deliberately, so a dataset scoring 5 with every gate measured and one scoring 5 with three gates never looked at received the same letter. Grade A was unreached and the page did not say why. `score_gates` also summed whatever keys it was handed, so a duplicated gate name could score 14 out of a stated maximum of 10 and buy an A.
corrections.after: A grade now states coverage as well as score. A requires all five gates scored and a score of at least 8; B requires at least three scored and at least 5. The reasoning string names how many were scored, every dataset ships a `gates_scored` count beside its grade, and the bundle carries a per-gate coverage tally. `score_gates` counts only the five named gates. The grade distribution is unchanged - B 14, C 116, X 15 - which is the point: the rule says what the letters already meant rather than reshuffling them.
corrections.why: The catalogue makes this concrete rather than hypothetical. Gate by gate, out of 145: provenance 144 scored, composition 6, contamination 1, yield 15, evidence 145. Evidence is PASS for every dataset because every catalogued dataset has been used by somebody, so it is two free points that discriminate nothing, and 125 of 145 records have two gates scored or fewer. For most of the corpus the only real signal is where the text came from. Grade A was therefore empty for a reason nobody had stated: not that nothing is good enough, but that nothing has been fully checked. The chapter now says so, and names the sharpest case - the contamination gate is scored on one dataset in the whole catalogue, and on none of the four the plan commits to. Those four clear licence, provenance and size; they are not datasets somebody finished checking, and a reader deciding whether to trust the plan needs that in front of them rather than derivable from an appendix.
corrections.source: Measured in this repository: dataframework/grade.py, web/data.json gate_coverage

corrections.before: The eight guardrails in `mix.py` were presented in one voice. The repetition constants cited a fitted curve to three significant figures; the composition constants cited nothing. `MAX_SYNTHETIC_SHARE_OF_INDIC = 0.50` carried the comment "past this, the 'Indic' tier is mostly manufactured text", which restates what 0.50 means and says nothing about why fifty. The page then reported the mixture breaching two of these lines without saying what kind of lines they were.
corrections.after: Every guardrail states its basis and how strong that basis is, and the bundle ships them so the page can show it. Four are published findings or a fitted curve from the repetition literature. One is adopted - the protected lane's 8% floor is what LightningLM reserved on its own corpus, not a measured optimum for this one. Three are asserted: the 20% lane ceiling has no source anywhere, the 1% minimum tier share is our own line loosely motivated by a finding about up-sampling 0.1% slivers, and the 50% synthetic cap appears once, in a risk register's mitigation column, phrased as "cap synthetic at ~50%" with no citation and no experiment. The strength maps onto provenance, so a measured guardrail wears the mark that means somebody ran it and an asserted one does not.
corrections.why: Pankaj asked where the 50% came from, which nothing in the code could answer. It came from docs/ATLAS.md risk R02 and it is a rule of thumb, and both lines this mixture crosses turn out to be in the asserted group. That does not excuse the breach - it changes what the breach means, from "we exceeded a measured limit" to "we exceeded a line we drew ourselves and have never tested". Presented identically, a judgment somebody wrote down and a constant somebody measured are indistinguishable to a reader, which is the confusion the rest of this page exists to prevent. One further gap surfaced while tracing it: R02 prescribes four mitigations against synthetic collapse and only the cap is implemented - the KenLM-perplexity floor, the n-gram diversity floor and the per-language entropy monitor are recorded as prose and checked by nothing. The page now says that too.
corrections.source: docs/ATLAS.md risk R02; arXiv:2606.07404; arXiv:2305.16264; dataframework/mix.py

corrections.before: Chapter 2 took its pool from the mixture's `unique_tokens` field and said of it: "Read once, this is the entire natural Indian-language pool - every verified corpus anyone has assembled, added together." At the recommended budget that field is 336B. The chapter's whole argument followed from it: the pool is large, four passes are nearly free, so the Indian share is reachable.
corrections.after: The pool is summed from the catalogue, the same source the datasets chapter reads: 84.9B, being Sangraha's verified portion and IndicCorp v2. The field is renamed `unique_tokens_required` everywhere, because that is what it is. Chapter 2 now says four passes on the real pool are worth 316B - 24% of what the tier is allocated - and that filling the allocation takes about 16 passes, which is the half-life the published fit names, at which the tokens are worth 66% of what they cost.
corrections.why: `unique_tokens` was never a measurement. milestones.py computes it as share x budget / epochs, so at 16.8T the indic-natural tier's 8% share over 4 epochs produced 336B: the pool the mixture would need in order for the share it wants to work. A demand figure wearing the clothes of a supply figure, and the page stated it as an inventory in the most explicit words available. Two things hid it. The growth chapter had it right all along - "336B of unique natural Indian text this stage asks for, 4.0x SHORT" - so the page contradicted itself across two chapters with the same number. And risk R19 records a 250-500B estimate for the real pool, which 336B sits inside, so the figure looked corroborated; R19 also calls that estimate "the single most important unverified number in the entire document". The agreement was a coincidence of arithmetic. The corrected chapter is a stronger one: "nearly free" was true of a pool four times larger than the one anybody holds.
corrections.source: dataframework/milestones.py; web/data.json sourcing; records/risks.json R19

corrections.before: The page recorded, in correction X15, that repetition is the weakest answer to a scarce pool and that the frontier rephrases instead - and then went on planning around passes, because nobody had costed the alternative. Chapter 2 ended on how many times to read the pool. Chapter 13's queue did not mention rephrasing at all.
corrections.after: The rephrasing route is costed and carried in both chapters. Restating the 84.9B committable pool twice makes it 170B and lifts what the tier is worth by about 25% at identical seen tokens, for a generation cost that stays under 1% of the run however the throughput is estimated. Chapter 2 says so where it used to end on passes; chapter 13 prices it beside the speech route, with its three limits.
corrections.why: The finding is that it is worth doing and is not the answer. At two variants - the only depth Kimi K2 uses in production - the tier is still 13% filled by unique text and 87% by repetition. Filling it with unique text would take sixteen variants, past anything anybody has reported. And whether a rephrasing counts as a distinct document for the repetition curve has never been measured; the 25% assumes it does, and nothing published says what the penalty is if it does not. So the honest conclusion is that the cheapest real lever improves the slice and leaves the gap, which makes it the strongest argument for funding collection - the argument that survives having tried the alternative. Cost is shown as a band rather than a figure, with the arithmetic stated: the throughput term spans an order of magnitude because decode is bound by weight reads rather than FLOPs, so a point estimate would claim a precision this project does not have.
corrections.source: arXiv:2507.20534 (Kimi K2); arXiv:2607.24653 (K3); Muennighoff Eq. 18 applied here

corrections.before: Supply was reported as raw sums of dataset token counts. The page printed 61T reachable and 363% of budget, 54.6T unlocked by four letters, and 84.9B of committable natural Indic. Nemotron-CC (v1) sat in one list and Nemotron-CC-v2 in another and both were added. The code row recorded 377M tokens.
corrections.after: Every sum over catalogue tokens now reports what survives deduplication as well as the raw figure, through one shared helper rather than a patch per call site - there were ten sum sites and fixing one is how this kind of error persists. Nemotron-CC-v2 contains v1, stated by NVIDIA, so the contained row is dropped from the sum outright. The code row is 747.4B, from its own dataset card. Stage 3 now reads 55.4T raw, 11.1T-22.2T after dedup, 66-132% of a 16.8T budget - a possible shortfall where it read 363% of budget.
corrections.why:
Risk R01 has been on this page throughout, severity high, called "the single most likely schedule-breaker": 60-80% cross-corpus duplication, because every large corpus here is a differently-filtered view of the same crawls. FineWeb is 96 Common Crawl dumps, FinePDFs 106 of them, Nemotron-CC is Common Crawl, HPLT v3.0 is 45% Common Crawl by volume. The plan summed them anyway and reported the total as available supply, which is the error R01 exists to warn about. Two distinct mechanisms now do the work and they are not interchangeable: exact containment is subtracted, because a publisher stated it; unknown overlap gets a range, because nobody has measured it. Facts get subtracted, uncertainty gets a band, and per-pair overlap coefficients are not invented to make the arithmetic look more precise than the evidence.

The Indic pool needed a different answer and is treated separately. R01's range is about Common Crawl, and Sangraha's verified portion is scraped from human-checked sites, OCR and transcription - sources a crawl does not reach - which is why it is the verified portion. What is unmeasured there is narrower: Sangraha Verified and IndicCorp v2 are both AI4Bharat scrapes of Indian websites with no published cross-deduplication, so 84.9B is a ceiling rather than a count, and the page says so.
corrections.source: risk R01; NVIDIA Nemotron-CC-v2 and Nemotron-Pretraining-Code-v1 dataset cards; FineWeb, FinePDFs and HPLT 3.0 documentation; IndicLLMSuite arXiv:2403.06350

corrections.before: Chart labels were truncated with an ellipsis. Fourteen across the page were losing text, up to 82px of it: "natural Indic we h...", and every tool name in the cleaning chapter, which appears nowhere else on the page.
corrections.after: Labels wrap. Where a grid had a fixed or auto track beside a flexible one, the flexible column was absorbing the whole shortfall and reaching zero - 4px at 900px, 28px at 1180px, which stacks letters vertically and is worse than the truncation. The rows now collapse on a container query against their own column rather than the viewport.
corrections.why: An ellipsis is honest only when the full text is reachable another way. A catalogue row is a button that opens the dataset's five gates, so it keeps its ellipsis; a chart label has no such escape and the information is simply gone. The container query matters because the figure column is narrow in two disjoint viewport bands - 761-1080px, and again above 1180px where the fixed rail takes 260px - so breakpoints fixed one and left the other. Asking whether there is room in this box holds at widths nobody thought to test.
corrections.source: measured in this repository across 390-1600px

corrections.before: The catalogue said nothing about how its datasets relate to each other. FineWeb's 15T sat beside FineWeb-Edu's 1.3T with nothing to say the second is inside the first, and the same for FinePDFs and FinePDFs-Edu, and for Nemotron-CC and its v2. A reader adding any of those pairs would be double-counting and the page gave them no way to know.
corrections.after: Fifteen datasets carry a published relationship, in four kinds that are deliberately not interchangeable: contained_by (3 pairs, stated by their publishers, subtracted from any sum holding the parent), additional_to (1, recorded because Nemotron-CC-v2.1 is genuinely additive and should not be 'fixed' into a containment), shares_source (7, real overlap of unpublished size), and independent (2, because 'these do not overlap' is as much a finding as the reverse). Two are unknown. Each carries a note stating what is concretely known - crawl counts, date ranges, modality - and the citation for it, both shown on hover beside the dataset's name. The containment map the sums use is read from these records rather than hand-kept, so the label a reader sees and the arithmetic are one statement.
corrections.why: Where the relationship is published it is recorded exactly; where only the existence of overlap is published, the label says so and the magnitude comes from risk R01's range alone. No per-pair overlap coefficient is invented, because nobody has measured one and a made-up fraction wearing the authority of a computation would be worse than the honest band. The callouts carry what can be said instead: FinePDFs draws on the same 106 Common Crawl dumps as FineWeb but takes the PDFs rather than the HTML, so its overlap is far smaller than the shared source implies; CulturaX is not built from the crawl directly but from mC4 and OSCAR, which both were; Sangraha's unverified portion comes from 'existing multilingual corpora', unnamed and unresolvable, which is why it is excluded rather than modelled.
corrections.source: dataset cards for fineweb, fineweb-edu, finepdfs, finepdfs-edu, Nemotron-CC-v2, Nemotron-CC-v2.1, Nemotron-Pretraining-Code-v1, CulturaX, sangraha, IndicCorpV2; arXiv:2511.01066 (HPLT 3.0); arXiv:2403.06350 (IndicLLMSuite)

corrections.before: Two blocks in the bundle declared one provenance over a mixture of exact counts and estimated sums, and both resolved it downward. The lifecycle block was marked `estimated` because one of its seven fields, `tokens_known`, sums catalogue size estimates — so "4 of 24 post-training datasets state a size", which is counted from records we hold, rendered under the same hedge as a projection. The orphan-tier block was marked `estimated` because it prices each orphan in GPU-hours and rupees, so the claim the page actually makes from it — that every tier in the mixture has at least one test that would notice it going missing — was hedged too, though it is a match against the benchmark register and nothing more.
corrections.after: Provenance is declared at the level the figure is actually made at. The lifecycle block declares `measured` over its counts and `tokens_known` carries its own `estimated` mark inline, naming the sum it comes from. The orphan block keeps `estimated` for the costs and gains a `counts` sub-block declaring `measured` over the two figures that are matched rather than priced: how many tiers were checked, and how many have no detector.
corrections.why: Under-claiming is the safe direction of the two and that is why it survived this long, but it is not free. A provenance mark is only worth reading if it varies with the evidence; hedging a count that a miscount would make a bug rather than an estimate spends the reader's trust in the mark to buy nothing. The bare-number invariant could not catch either one — it inherits provenance down the tree and so proves only that every number carries a mark, never that the mark is the right one. Both blocks passed it before and after.
corrections.source: dataframework.sourcing.build_lifecycle; dataframework.export, orphan_tiers block

corrections.before: X26 recorded that a subset must not be summed beside the set containing it, and wired the containment map into the browser so the stage registers would apply it. The wiring never fired. `contained_by` maps a child to a *list* of parents - a dataset can sit inside more than one - and the filter tested that list for membership in a set of ids, which is false for every list there has ever been. So every stage's reachable total was the plain sum: Nemotron-CC v1's 6.30T counted once on its own and again inside Nemotron-CC-v2's 6.60T, and the same for FineWeb-Edu inside FineWeb and FinePDFs-Edu inside FinePDFs wherever a stage reached both. The comment above the line described the subtraction correctly throughout.
corrections.after: The filter asks whether any one of a child's parents is present, which is the rule the multiple-parent case needs and the rule the comment always claimed. The Python guard that proves a subset is never summed with its parent had passed all along, because the summing happens in the browser and the guard was only ever pointed at the bundle.
corrections.why: The lesson is not the array-versus-scalar slip, it is where the guard was aimed. A test that watches the producer cannot see a consumer that ignores what the producer ships. The map was correct in data.json for as long as the page was wrong on screen, and nothing in the suite could tell the two apart.
corrections.source: web/chapters.js, dropContained in the stage register; data.sourcing.contained_by

corrections.before: The catalogue described availability in prose copied from a seed cell, and 'open' in that cell turned out to mean three different things: fetch it freely, click through terms, or ask a person at the publisher and wait. Nothing distinguished them, so datasets requiring NVIDIA's approval sat in the same band as ones you can wget. Two figures were wrong as a result. COD-02 was one row covering Nemotron-Pretraining-Code v1, v2 and v3 and counted 747.4B as committable today - but v1 and v2 are gated on manual approval, and v3, the only ungated one, holds 173B and says it is incremental to the other two. And ENG-11 was 'Dolma' with no version and no size while AI2 had shipped Dolma 3, a 6T ungated ODC-By mix, so a corpus larger than anything in the committable band counted as nothing at all.
corrections.after: Each dataset's distribution point is read from the publisher rather than the seed row, and carries HuggingFace's own three-way gating value with the date it was checked. Manual gating is a blocker distinct from the licence; click-through gating is recorded but is not a blocker, because accepting terms is something you do unilaterally. Nemotron-CC-v2 moves from one letter away to two, which is the honest answer to why the older v1 is the committable one. COD-02 counts 173B. Dolma is Dolma 3 at 6T, unresolved on licence rather than invisible.
corrections.why: The page's whole dividing line is whether anybody's permission is needed, and it was sorting on a field that could not see permission. The legal chapter now also states the thing the green marks never said: a web corpus's licence covers the curation, not the copyright of the text inside it, which never left the sites it was crawled from - so a permitted mark means the curator allows redistribution of their package, not that anyone may train on its contents. Common Crawl's own terms grant use of the service, require respect for third-party copyright, demand indemnity, and advise counsel before commercial use.
corrections.source: huggingface.co/api/datasets for each row, checked 2026-08-06; nvidia/Nemotron-Pretraining-Code-v3 card ('146 M new files (173 B tokens)', 'meant to be used jointly with the v2 and v1 corpora'); allenai/dolma3_mix-6T card; commoncrawl.org/terms-of-use

corrections.before: The mix was described only by where text came from. Tiers name a provenance - english-web-hq, indic-natural - and `kind` splits them into skills and knowledge, but nothing said what a token was *for*, and nothing said what it was *about*. So the growth ladder could describe four stages without ever saying what each one teaches, and the catalogue could report 145 datasets without anyone being able to ask whether it covers news, or literature, or agriculture.
corrections.after: Two lenses added over the same tokens, deliberately not merged with the tier: a modality says what kind of thinking a token teaches, a domain says what it is about. The seven modalities and the code language list are the specification's own, carried verbatim including that agentic_traces is owned by Team 17 and its format is still pending - a modality nobody has agreed a format for cannot be collected, and the plan should say whose decision that is. Each stage of the ladder now shows the modality mix it is taught in, following the order a person is taught in: language, then the world, then symbols, then the things that need all three. General text falls 62% to 29% across the four stages while code rises 6% to 26%.
corrections.why: The coverage report is the half that matters, because it is counted rather than proposed. Of 16 domains the curriculum names, 12 have a dataset that isolates them, 2 (social, qa) exist only as an unseparated slice of a web crawl - trainable but not weightable, measurable or holdable-out - and 2 have nothing in the catalogue at all: agriculture and health. Agriculture is the uncomfortable one for an India-first model, being the sector most of the country works in. Counting only what could be committed today rather than what is catalogued, 2 of the 16 domains have even one dataset clear of every blocker. Each row ships the pattern it was matched by, so the count is checkable rather than asserted. The tier weights and curriculum emphases are typed `estimated` and named as this framework's proposal: nobody has classified a crawl by modality, and a plan dressed as a measurement would be the exact failure this register exists to catch.
corrections.source: dataframework.modalities; counted from catalog.json at build time

tools.name: Setu
tools.why: Spark-based distributed cleaning/dedup/filtering pipeline purpose-built for Indian scripts (PDF, web, speech extraction), from AI4Bharat, MIT-licensed. The document calls it 'arguably as valuable as the data itself' and says to adopt or fork it rather than rebuild; the Section 17 pipeline uses it at the quality-filtering stage alongside forked FineWeb-2 configs.
tools.note: Listed in the Section 17 tool table as 'Indic-specific cleaning/dedup at scale', so it spans filtering and dedup; the pipeline diagram places it under QUALITY FILTERING, which is the stage recorded here. AI4Bharat also used it to re-clean CulturaX.

tools.name: datatrove
tools.why: Hugging Face's general-purpose data processing library, Apache-2.0, listed in the Section 17 'tools you should adopt rather than rebuild' table.
tools.note: The document assigns it the generic need 'general-purpose data processing' rather than one pipeline box; filtering is the closest stage in this schema.

tools.name: NeMo Curator
tools.why: NVIDIA's curation stack for GPU-scale data curation, Apache-2.0, listed in the Section 17 adopt-rather-than-rebuild table.
tools.note: Stage recorded as filtering; the document's need column says 'curation at GPU scale', which spans filtering and dedup.

tools.name: GlotLID
tools.why: Open, script-aware language ID with 2000+ labels; the Section 17 pipeline runs a GlotLID ensemble as the LANGUAGE & SCRIPT ID stage across Devanagari, Bengali, Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam, Gurmukhi, Gujarati, Odia, Perso-Arabic, Meitei Mayek, Ol Chiki and Latin. FineWeb-2 already uses it for per-language tuned filters.
tools.note: Code-mix and romanisation detection sit in the same stage — the document treats Hinglish as a first-class language, not noise — but names no specific tool for it.

tools.name: trafilatura
tools.why: Named in the Section 17 pipeline as an HTML-to-text extractor for the EXTRACTION stage.
tools.note: Named only in the pipeline diagram, not in the Section 17 tool table, so the document gives no licence or explicit adopt/build verdict; 'adopt' is inferred from its being listed as the pipeline's chosen extractor.

tools.name: resiliparse
tools.why: Named in the Section 17 pipeline alongside trafilatura as an HTML-to-text extractor for the EXTRACTION stage.
tools.note: As with trafilatura, named only in the pipeline diagram; no licence or explicit verdict is stated in the document.

tools.name: olmOCR / olmOCR-2
tools.why: Addendum A.2 is an explicit material correction: on 300 real printed Devanagari scans, olmOCR-7B falls to 40.5 chrF++ — the worst-in-class result of ten benchmarked systems, from the model behind olmOCR-Bench — while all ten cluster at 91-98 on clean rendered text. The main document's 'fine-tune olmOCR for Indic scripts' recommendation is withdrawn; Qwen3-VL-8B (75.2) is the recommended alternative base.
tools.note: Section 17's tool table and Sections 9/19 still list olmOCR as the OCR tool to adopt (Apache-2.0, arXiv:2510.19817). Addendum A explicitly overrides Sections 1-21 where they conflict, so the verdict here is 'avoid'. Benchmark source: arXiv:2606.29213, published 28 June 2026.

tools.name: Qwen3-VL-8B
tools.why: The winner among open models on the real-scan Devanagari stress test at 75.2 chrF++, beating GPT-5.5 (58.5) and olmOCR-7B (40.5), and it runs on a single 24 GB GPU. Addendum A.2's revised recommendation is to build the Indic OCR pipeline on it, report median and catastrophic-failure-rate rather than mean, and validate exclusively on real scans.
tools.note: Source: arXiv:2606.29213. The document also notes Apache-2.0-class generators are preferred for anything redistributable, to avoid synthetic-data licence-chain problems.

tools.name: DeepSeek-OCR
tools.why: Has the best median of any system in the Devanagari stress test, but suffers rare catastrophic repetition failures — outputs up to 71x reference length — that destroy its mean. Addendum A.2's revised recommendation names Qwen3-VL-8B, not DeepSeek-OCR, as the pipeline base.
tools.note: The document issues no explicit adopt/avoid verdict for DeepSeek-OCR; 'avoid' is inferred from the catastrophic-failure finding plus the explicit recommendation of a different base model. Its strong median is a genuine reason to revisit if the failure mode can be detected and retried.

tools.name: IndicConformer
tools.why: AI4Bharat's ASR model covering all 22 scheduled languages, surfaced in Addendum A.5 as coverage the main document understated. Needed for the Section 8 high-leverage move: transcribing the open Indic speech pool, which Addendum A.5 revises upward from ~35,000 hours to well north of 100,000 hours across BhasaAnuvaad, IndicVoices, Vaani, SPRING-INX, Shrutilipi, Kathbath, SYSPIN and Rasa.
tools.note: Listed in Addendum A.5 as available from the AI4Bharat HF org; no licence string is given for the model itself in the document.

tools.name: IndicSeamless
tools.why: SeamlessM4T-v2 fine-tuned on BhasaAnuvaad; stated as SOTA for Indic speech-to-text translation, beating cascaded approaches on FLEURS and BhasaAnuvaad-test.
tools.note: From Addendum A.5's correction table (AI4Bharat HF org). Relevant where transcription and translation are combined; no licence string is given in the document.

tools.name: IndicASR / Whisper-Indic fine-tune
tools.why: The Section 17 pipeline specifies ASR at the EXTRACTION stage as 'IndicASR / Whisper-Indic FT' — a fine-tune you produce, not an off-the-shelf adoption. It feeds recommended action 5: ASR-transcribe all the open Indic speech, which the document says nobody else has done at scale and which produces text that exists nowhere else.
tools.note: The document names no specific released Whisper-Indic checkpoint; SCRIBE (arXiv:2605.20712) is flagged as useful diagnostic evaluation for this pipeline.

tools.name: KenLM perplexity filter (vs a Sangraha-verified reference)
tools.why: The Section 17 QUALITY FILTERING box specifies KenLM perplexity scored against a Sangraha-verified reference; BhashaKritika's modular QC pipeline (script/language ID, n-gram repetition, KenLM perplexity) is cited as the reason synthetic Indic converged faster than noisy web Indic. Section 18.1 also makes KenLM-perplexity floors part of the anti-synthetic-collapse mitigation.
tools.note: Reference model must be trained per language against the Sangraha-verified tier — the document treats this as something you construct, not adopt.

tools.name: FineWeb-Edu-style per-language quality classifier
tools.why: The Section 17 pipeline calls for a model-based classifier 'trained per-lang'. Addendum B.2 warns these classifiers carry the same English-proxy bias that made OPUS under-value Indic data (golden-proxy cosine 0.876 with the English web band), so the Always-ON lane of ~8% of every batch must bypass them entirely.
tools.note: FineWeb-2-HQ is cited as evidence the approach works — an XLM-R-based quality classifier keeping the top 10% matches full FineWeb-2 with 6x fewer tokens.

tools.name: Global MinHash + LSH deduplication
tools.why: Sangraha, CulturaX, MADLAD-400, FineWeb-2 and HPLT all derive from Common Crawl, so the document expects 60-80% cross-corpus duplication and requires global MinHash+LSH across the entire mix rather than per-corpus dedup — 'the difference between 20T tokens and 20T tokens of which 6T are unique'. Nemotron-CC's authors found FineWebEdu-2 and DCLM held roughly 80% fuzzy duplicates because they only did sharded approximate dedup.
tools.note: The pipeline runs exact SHA dedup first, then global MinHash+LSH. Section 18.1 rates 'global dedup collapses 23T to 9T, not 15T' as the single most likely schedule-breaker and prescribes running dedup on a 10% sample first. Addendum B.1 tempers this: dedup down to the unique pool, then choose repetition deliberately — dedup is not the same as see-once.

tools.name: SemDeDup
tools.why: Embedding-based semantic dedup, applied in the Section 17 pipeline to the top-quality tier after exact and fuzzy dedup.
tools.note: Named as a pipeline step only; the document gives no licence, owner or explicit adopt/build verdict, so 'adopt' reflects that it is specified as an existing technique to apply rather than something to invent.

tools.name: 13-gram overlap + MinHash decontamination against BENCHMARK_BLOCKLIST
tools.why: Section 12.3 Rule 1 mandates a BENCHMARK_BLOCKLIST holding the exact text of every evaluation item across every benchmark listed, with 13-gram overlap detection (the Llama/GPT convention) plus MinHash near-duplicate detection run against the entire pre-training corpus at every stage; any hit is dropped, not down-weighted, and every drop is logged with the benchmark it hit. Synthesised data re-enters the same gate.
tools.note: There is an existence proof at scale: LightningLM dropped its 31.3B-token B2 pool entirely for contamination and never trained on the golden proxy (Addendum B.2). No off-the-shelf tool is named — the document treats the blocklist and detector as project-built.

acquisition.effort: A letter - §15.4 prices it at '₹0 (a letter)'; §19 item 1 flags it as zero cost but the longest lead time, so send it in week 1
acquisition.why: Unlocks the entire K-12 curriculum in 36 languages. Highest ROI action available. §10.1: India's magnificent public educational corpus is CC BY-NC-ND (NCERT) and CC BY-NC-SA (DIKSHA) and therefore unusable in a commercial foundation model, and §14.1 point 4 stresses that the ANI fair-dealing ruling 'does not override contracts' - an NC licence is a contract, so only a grant dissolves it.
acquisition.note: One of the three ₹0 acquisitions §21 says are 'worth more than any amount of additional scraping, and should be initiated in week one'. §15.4: 'Items 1-3 are free and worth more than everything else combined.'

acquisition.effort: A formal data-sharing MoU. §3.6: 'Bharat Data Sagar is a partnership target, not a download... the single highest-leverage business-development action available to you, worth more than months of scraping.'
acquisition.why: ~20T tokens claimed, publicly funded. Public-interest framing helps. §3.6 sizes the public investment at ~₹1,293 crore (₹235 crore NM-ICPS + ₹1,058 crore MeitY / IndiaAI Mission).
acquisition.note: §15.4 states the cost as '₹0-small', not a flat zero; cost_inr is 0 as the stated floor. The 20T / ~3 petabyte figure is a [VENDOR CLAIM] - a CEO statement from Feb 2026, unaudited, and §A.7 rates it LOW confidence: 'Do not build a plan that depends on this being true.' The corpus itself is not publicly redistributable and models trained on it ship under a BharatGen non-commercial licence.

acquisition.effort: Submit the EOI to contribute (https://aikosh.indiaai.gov.in/static/datasets_EOI.pdf) and contribute your derived datasets
acquisition.why: Contribute your derived datasets, gain access + goodwill + compute credits. §3.7: AIKosh is the national aggregator - 10,262+ datasets, 292 models, 20 sectors, 394 contributing organisations - hosting IndicVoices, SPRING-INX and the EKA corpus, and providing GPU/CPU notebooks via AIRAWAT.
acquisition.note: Third of the three free actions in §21. §3.7 flags the catch: licensing is per-dataset and heterogeneous - 'you must build a per-dataset licence ingestion step - do not bulk download'.

acquisition.effort: Licensing conversations with 20-40 publishers; §15.3 advises negotiating a retrieval/grounding deal rather than a training deal - 'far cheaper, publishers accept it more readily, and for a conversational model it delivers most of the value'. §19 item 10 starts these at week 12+
acquisition.why: Natural, edited, high-register Indic text at a scale nothing else provides. §15.3: no single publisher has dominant leverage, so 'you do not need Times of India. You need forty regional-language publishers' - Dainik Jagran, Malayala Manorama, Eenadu, Daily Thanthi, Sakal, Anandabazar Patrika and the hundreds beneath them.

Dense rather than MoE, so active parameters equal total. Its tokenizer is measured in this repository and is the worst of the three multilingual candidates on Indian text (x2.49 mean tax against x1.66 for the best) — which is the cost a continue-pretraining route would inherit and could not undo.

Read from the Hugging Face model card `sarvamai/sarvam-30b` (§A.1). Active params 2.4B non-embedding; 128 experts, top-6 routing, 1 shared expert; grouped KV (num_key_value_heads=4), 19 layers; intermediate 8192 / moe_intermediate 1024; rope_theta 8e6 with no RoPE scaling; auxiliary-loss-free router balancing, routed scaling factor 2.5; The card states no token count; Sarvam's launch blog reports 16T. params_total is taken from the model name and §A.6's 'Sarvam AI (30B, 105B)' - the Atlas never states a total-parameter figure. context is null: the card details rope_theta but no context length for the 30B. Positioning: 'reliable coding ability, best-in-class conversational quality across Indian languages'; handles multilingual voice calls while performing tool calls. Public rollout 6 March 2026.

LICENCE CORRECTED BY ADDENDUM A.1 ('MATERIAL CORRECTION #1 - Sarvam-105B is Apache 2.0, with full architecture disclosed'), read from the Hugging Face model card `sarvamai/sarvam-105b`; the addendum wins where it conflicts with Sections 1-21, which had treated Sarvam only as a reference point rather than 'a licence-free starting position'. 128 experts, top-8 routing, 1 shared expert; MLA-style attention with decoupled QK (q_head_dim 192 RoPE+noPE split, v_head_dim 128, head_dim 576, hidden_size 4096); FFN intermediate 16384 / moe_intermediate 2048; YaRN scaling factor 40 for 128K context; auxiliary-loss-free router balancing, routed scaling factor 2.5; The card states no token count; Sarvam's launch blog reports 12T. params_total from the model name and §A.6. Consequences per §A.1: it can be upcycled toward ~300B, used as an Indic teacher with zero licence-chain contamination (the clean alternative to BhashaKritika), and it sets the public bar any new 300B must beat.

§B.4, from the LightningLM 0.1V technical report (arXiv:2606.07404), described as in-project. A 120B sparse MoE: 460 routed experts, top-12 routing, 5.93B active (~5% of 118.67B stored), grown in four stages from a 1.78B dense seed (1.78B -> 5B -> 9B -> 120B), trained end-to-end on a single eight-GPU node; early stages at 4K context and 9B+ at 8K, so context here is the 8K final-stage figure. Capstone economics quoted as ~67 days and ~$100K-class without spot pricing for the V4 run. Corpus (§B.2): 1,118B tokens across 33,353 shards, ~1,254B effective, with a 78.1B always-ON tier at 8% of every batch and 31.3B dropped for contamination. Licence is null - the Atlas never states one.

BharatGen. Pre-trained on ~22T tokens (§1.1). §18.1: 'Param-2 uses 64 experts with 2 shared for code-mixing/domain-mixing', and BharatGen reported MoE layers naturally grouping related languages (Hindi/Marathi). Released under a BharatGen non-commercial licence (§3.6, §13.1) - §13.1 notes this blocks distillation-based data generation. params_total and params_active are read off the model name (17B total / A2.4B active); the Atlas states no separate figures. Context length is not stated. Trained on Bharat Data Sagar, which is not publicly redistributable.
