milestones.requirement: Licence-clean sources only, and every one of them graded. What is read here is inherited by every model grown from it, so this is the rung where being right is both essential and affordable.

milestones.feasibility: Trivially achievable today. FineWeb-Edu (1.3T) + Nemotron-CC-v2 subset + Stack v2 (900B) + Sangraha (251B) + FinePDFs (3T) already overshoots.
milestones.requirement: §16.2 'Prove the recipe' (weeks 1-8): FineWeb-Edu (1.3T) + Nemotron-CC-v2 HQ subset (1.5T) + Stack v2 permissive (0.7T) + Nemotron-CC-Math (0.13T) + Sangraha full (0.25T) + BPCC/Samanantar/Aksharantar (0.05T) + FineWeb-2 Indic (0.04T) + multilingual (0.8T) + Common Pile (0.25T). Everything here is green-licence. Train a 7-15B dense proxy on this before touching the 300B.

milestones.feasibility: Conservative for the size: Gemma 3's 12B took 12T and Llama 3.1's 8B took 15T. The first rung the Indic pool cannot fill — 160B unique needed against 84.9B committable.
milestones.requirement: Web-scale English and code enter here, which is the point at which the licence questions in the catalogue stop being theoretical.

milestones.feasibility: Achievable in ~8-12 weeks of pipeline work. Requires global cross-corpus dedup, which typically removes 40-70%.
milestones.requirement: §16.2 'Safe production floor' (weeks 8-20): add full Nemotron-CC-v2 + v2.1, FinePDFs, FineWeb-2-HQ, full Stack v2 + Nemotron-Code, MegaMath + full math tier, HPLT 3.0 multilingual, 0.8T of your own Indic synthetic, and ASR transcription of all 35K hours of Indic speech. Still fully licence-clean if BhashaKritika is replicated rather than ingested. §1.2 frames this as the validated 'must-have' core underneath the 15T architecture.

milestones.feasibility: Achievable but requires manufacturing. You must generate 1.5-3T synthetic Indic tokens yourself (à la BhashaKritika's 540B, scaled up ~4x) plus heavy FinePDFs/FineTranslations use.
milestones.requirement: §16.2 'Recommended target' (weeks 20-40): add 2.4T Indic synthetic (scaled generation), FineTranslations both sides, a curriculum-generation tier across 22 languages x 5 difficulty levels, licensed regional-publisher archives, and translated Nemotron Diverse-QA into 22 Indic languages. §1.2's recommendation: 'architect for 15T, with a validated 10T must-have core and a 5T synthetic/expansion tier that can grow'; 15T unique tokens at ~35B active params is called a sane, defensible ratio. §16.1 gives the mix: ~23.4T raw -> ~15.0T after dedup, Indic total ~2.8T (18.7%) of which only 0.30T (2.0%) is naturally occurring.

milestones.feasibility: Derived, because the comparator does not disclose its own. Gemma 4's technical report and its model card both describe the training data without ever stating a token count; Gemma 3's card does state one, verbatim: the 27B was trained with 14 trillion tokens. 16.8T is that figure plus 20% for one generation of growth. It is a stated estimate with a stated method, not a published number, and it is labelled that way everywhere it appears.
milestones.requirement: Everything the 10T rung lists, plus the volume that only arrives when the licence questions are answered. This catalogue can commit 6.57T today, so the seed as specified is 10.2T short — and the shortfall is a stack of unwritten letters rather than a collection problem.

milestones.feasibility: Achievable only with aggressive multi-epoch reuse + very large synthetic generation + PDF/OCR/ASR pipelines that don't exist off-the-shelf for Indic. BharatGen claims to be here [VENDOR CLAIM] but the corpus is not redistributable.
milestones.requirement: §16.2 'Stretch, phase 2': OCR of India's print archive at scale (an Indic-script OCR model), a BharatGen/Bharat Data Sagar data agreement, 2 epochs on the highest-quality 30% of the mix, and materially expanded synthetic generation. 'Do not plan the first training run around 20T' - reach it in a continued-pretraining phase. Addendum B.1 revises this from hand-waved to quantified: 20T processed ~= 11-13T unique plus a scheduled epoch plan concentrated on the scarce, high-value tiers (Muennighoff: up to 4 epochs is almost as good as fresh data; R*_D ~= 15).

milestones.feasibility: Frontier scale, and the rung where collection rather than compute is the whole problem. Llama 4 trained on over 30T; Qwen3 on 36T across 119 languages. Every extra trillion beyond the seed comes from English, code and multilingual web text, all of which is purchasable or already open.
milestones.requirement: Nothing in the Indian-language plan changes at this rung, which is the finding rather than an omission. The natural Indic pool contributes the same absolute quantity it always did, so the India share falls purely by growing. Holding it requires funding the acquisition queue, not the crawl budget.

legal.title: ANI v. OpenAI — first Indian judicial ruling on AI training
legal.detail: ANI (Asian News International) sued OpenAI in November 2024, alleging OpenAI used ANI's news reports without permission to train ChatGPT, and separately that ChatGPT fabricated stories attributed to ANI. The Digital News Publishers Association and the Federation of Indian Publishers intervened. The Delhi High Court refused the interim injunction; the suit continues to trial on the merits.
legal.status: interim — injunction refused, suit continues to trial
legal.action: Treat the outcome as favourable but provisional: build on it, do not bet the corpus architecture on it surviving trial or appeal.
legal.source: Delhi High Court, Justice Amit Bansal, judgment 24 July 2026, 135 pages (§14.1)
legal.note: §14 opens: "This section changed materially four days before this document was written." §A.7 grades the ruling high confidence — "multiple independent legal and business outlets" — and §20 lists the coverage as Business Standard, LawBeat, The New Publishing Standard. The document cites no case number or neutral citation.

legal.title: Training held prima facie fair dealing for research
legal.detail: OpenAI's storage and use of ANI's content to train its models is prima facie protected as "fair dealing" for "private or personal use, including research".
legal.status: prima facie finding at the interim-injunction stage
legal.action: You may rely on it as the current Indian position on ingestion for training, while keeping the corpus decomposable in case it is re-examined.
legal.source: Section 52(1)(a)(i) of the Copyright Act, 1957, as applied in ANI v. OpenAI, 24 July 2026 (§14.1)
legal.note: §14.1 also states this stretch of Section 52(1)(a)(i) "is the entire legal foundation" for training in India — see L12.

legal.title: ANI failed to establish memorisation or reproduction
legal.detail: ANI failed to establish that ChatGPT memorised or reproduced its copyrighted news reports.
legal.status: prima facie finding at the interim-injunction stage
legal.action: Run and document memorisation testing so you can affirmatively demonstrate low memorisation — see L26.
legal.source: ANI v. OpenAI, Delhi High Court, 24 July 2026 (§14.1)

legal.title: Copyright protects expression, not facts
legal.detail: Copyright protects expression, not the underlying facts or information — "news of the day" is not protected.
legal.status: prima facie finding at the interim-injunction stage
legal.source: ANI v. OpenAI, Delhi High Court, 24 July 2026 (§14.1)

legal.title: Commercial entities not automatically excluded from fair dealing
legal.detail: The court rejected the argument that commercial entities are automatically excluded from claiming the fair-dealing defence.
legal.status: prima facie finding at the interim-injunction stage
legal.source: ANI v. OpenAI, Delhi High Court, 24 July 2026 (§14.1)
legal.note: Commentary summarised in the document treats this as one of the ruling's vulnerabilities on appeal — see L08.

legal.title: Practical effect — evidentiary burden shifts to publishers
legal.detail: The burden has shifted onto publishers to prove memorisation or reproduction, not merely ingestion — a considerably harder evidentiary bar. For an India-based project this is a meaningfully favourable environment relative to 12 months ago. "It is not a licence to scrape indiscriminately."
legal.action: Do not read the ruling as permission to scrape; keep the risk-tiered corpus and compliance gate regardless.
legal.source: ANI v. OpenAI, Delhi High Court, 24 July 2026 (§14.1)

legal.title: Limit 1 — these are prima facie findings
legal.detail: The judgment expressly states the findings do not control the final outcome. Discovery, expert evidence and trial are still ahead.
legal.action: Do not architect anything that only works if these findings hold.
legal.source: ANI v. OpenAI, 24 July 2026 — §14.1 "What it does NOT mean" item 1

legal.title: Limit 2 — single-judge interim order, appealable
legal.detail: It is a single-judge interim order; an appellate bench could land differently. Serious commentary has already identified vulnerabilities: that the court treated an internal technical process as "private use" even where the objective purpose is a public commercial product; that it applied Canadian "research" jurisprudence to differently-worded Indian text; and that it arguably used updating construction to create a commercial AI-training exception that Parliament did not enact.
legal.action: Keep the clean tier separable so a compliant base model can be retrained if the ruling is reversed on appeal.
legal.source: ANI v. OpenAI, 24 July 2026 — §14.1 "What it does NOT mean" item 2; mitigation in §18.2
legal.note: The document names no commentator or publication for the "serious commentary".

legal.title: Limit 3 — the hallucination / false-attribution claim is unresolved
legal.detail: ANI's suit always had two limbs; only the training limb was addressed. The hallucination/false-attribution claim remains unresolved.
legal.source: ANI v. OpenAI, 24 July 2026 — §14.1 "What it does NOT mean" item 3
legal.note: This is item 3 of the document's own five-item list. The document does not state which regime the false-attribution limb sounds in (passing off, defamation, or otherwise).

legal.title: Limit 4 — it does not override contracts
legal.detail: A NonCommercial licence (NCERT, DIKSHA, NPTEL) is a contract, not a copyright default. Fair dealing does not let you ignore it.
legal.action: Exclude NC-licensed corpora from a commercial model, or licence them — see L31 and L28.
legal.source: ANI v. OpenAI, 24 July 2026 — §14.1 "What it does NOT mean" item 4

legal.title: Limit 5 — it does not touch the DPDP Act
legal.detail: Copyright and data protection are separate regimes; the ruling says nothing about DPDP obligations.
legal.action: Run the DPDP compliance programme independently of any copyright analysis.
legal.source: ANI v. OpenAI, 24 July 2026 — §14.1 "What it does NOT mean" item 5
legal.note: §14.2 adds that for an India-based training run "data protection is a bigger operational constraint than copyright".

legal.title: India has no explicit TDM exception — the statute was stretched
legal.detail: Unlike the EU (DSM Directive Arts. 3–4) or Japan (Art. 30-4), Indian copyright law is right-holder-centric with a closed list of fair-dealing purposes. The ANI ruling stretched Section 52(1)(a)(i) to cover training. "That stretch is the entire legal foundation, and it is one appeal away from re-examination."
legal.status: no statutory TDM exception; judicial stretch only
legal.action: Assume the foundation can move; keep the corpus decomposable and the clean tier trainable on its own.
legal.source: §14.1, closing paragraph (Copyright Act 1957 s.52(1)(a)(i); EU DSM Directive Arts. 3–4; Japan Art. 30-4)
legal.note: This point sits in its own paragraph in §14.1, outside the numbered five-item "What it does NOT mean" list — so the document actually states six distinct limits on the ruling, not five.

legal.title: You are a Data Fiduciary
legal.detail: You determine the purpose and means of processing training data, so you are a Data Fiduciary. Obligations attach even when data comes from third parties or is processed on external infrastructure.
legal.action: Accept Data Fiduciary duties for the whole pipeline, including third-party corpora and external compute.
legal.source: DPDP Act 2023 + DPDP Rules 2025 (§14.2)
legal.note: §14.2 frames the whole regime: "For an India-based training run, data protection is a bigger operational constraint than copyright."

legal.title: Consent-centric processing
legal.detail: Free, specific, informed consent per specified purpose; notices must itemise the personal data collected and the exact purpose.
legal.action: Itemise personal data and purpose in the notice; do not rely on generic blanket consent.
legal.source: DPDP Act 2023 + DPDP Rules 2025 (§14.2)
legal.note: The document does not state how consent is to be obtained for web-scraped personal data — that gap is what makes the "publicly available" exemption (L16) load-bearing.

legal.title: Erasure obligation — implies selective removal and arguably unlearning
legal.detail: Data must be erased when consent is withdrawn or the purpose is served. This implies the ability to selectively remove data from training pipelines and logs — and, arguably, to handle machine unlearning. Requests must be addressed within 90 days.
legal.action: Build an erasure-request index (document hash → shard → checkpoint lineage) on day one; retrofitting provenance into a 15T-token corpus is effectively impossible.
legal.source: DPDP Act 2023; 90-day deadline at Rule 14, DPDP Rules 2025 (§14.2)
legal.note: The document says machine unlearning is "arguably" required — it does not claim the Act or Rules mandate it expressly.

legal.title: "Publicly available" exemption — scope contested
legal.detail: Section 3(c)(ii) excludes personal data the data principal made publicly available, but the scope is contested. MeitY stated in the Rajya Sabha (Aug 2024) that scraping publicly available user data remains subject to the IT Act, IT Rules and DPDP Act including consent and transparency obligations — which "sits uneasily with the plain text". IAMAI formally petitioned MeitY in August 2025 seeking an explicit AI-training exemption under Section 17(5). As of this writing, no such blanket exemption has been notified.
legal.status: contested — no exemption notified as of 28 July 2026
legal.action: Do not treat "it was public" as a complete answer; keep consent and transparency obligations live for scraped personal data.
legal.source: DPDP Act 2023 s.3(c)(ii); MeitY statement in the Rajya Sabha, Aug 2024; IAMAI petition to MeitY, Aug 2025 seeking s.17(5) exemption (§14.2)

legal.title: Research exemption is purpose-based and may not cover commercial training
legal.detail: Section 17(2)(b) conditionally exempts research processing — but exemptions are purpose-based, and commercial model training is not obviously research.
legal.action: Do not plan on the research exemption for a commercial training run.
legal.note: Recorded as a limit rather than an obligation: it constrains a defence, it does not impose a duty. Note the tension with the copyright side, where the ANI ruling accepted training as "research" under the Copyright Act (L02) — the document does not reconcile the two.

legal.title: Children's data — verifiable parental consent, no profiling
legal.detail: Verifiable parental consent is required for under-18s; no tracking, profiling, or behavioural targeting of children. "For a model trained on educational content this is directly relevant."
legal.action: Add children's-data detection and exclusion to the ingestion gate.
legal.source: DPDP Act 2023 s.9 / Rule 10, DPDP Rules 2025 (§14.2)

legal.title: Cross-border transfer restricted to notified countries
legal.detail: Transfers are permitted to notified countries. Relevant if you train on non-Indian cloud.
legal.action: Check the notified-country list before choosing non-Indian training infrastructure.
legal.source: DPDP Act 2023 s.16 / Rule 15, DPDP Rules 2025 (§14.2)
legal.note: The document does not say which countries are notified.

legal.title: Ingestion gate — PII and India-specific ID detection
legal.detail: The ingestion gate must do PII detection and redaction (names, phones, emails, addresses), India-specific ID pattern detection (Aadhaar, PAN, passport, voter ID, bank), and children's-data detection and exclusion.
legal.action: Build automated Aadhaar/PAN/passport-pattern detectors into ingestion; redact PII and exclude children's data before anything reaches the corpus.
legal.source: §14.2 "Operational requirements this imposes on your pipeline"; §13.4 ("Any government/personal/financial identity documents"); §17 SAFETY & COMPLIANCE GATE
legal.note: The §17 pipeline diagram restates the same gate: "PII redaction · Aadhaar/PAN/passport/bank pattern detection", CSAM hash matching, toxicity, children's-data exclusion, licence tag propagation.

legal.title: Provenance record per document
legal.detail: Keep a provenance record for every document: source URL, licence, retrieval date, hash.
legal.action: Emit a per-document provenance record at ingestion; do not defer it.
legal.source: §14.2 operational-requirements block; §17 SAFETY & COMPLIANCE GATE

legal.title: Erasure-request index (hash → shard → checkpoint lineage)
legal.detail: Maintain an erasure-request index mapping document hash → shard → checkpoint lineage. "The erasure-request index is the part teams skip and later regret. Build it on day one; retrofitting provenance into a 15T-token corpus is effectively impossible."
legal.action: Build the index before the first large ingestion run.
legal.source: §14.2 operational-requirements block; mitigation repeated in §18.2 ("DPDP erasure request against training data")

legal.title: Posture 1 — tier the corpus by risk and prove the clean tier first
legal.detail: Tier your corpus by risk exactly as this document does: build the clean tier first and prove the model works on it.
legal.action: Build and validate on the clean tier before touching restricted material.
legal.source: §14.3 "A defensible legal posture (not legal advice)", item 1

legal.title: Posture 2 — honour robots.txt, noai/noimageai, and TDM reservation signals
legal.detail: Honour robots.txt, `noai`/`noimageai` meta tags, and TDM reservation signals. "Even without a statutory obligation, ignoring them converts an arguable case into a wilful one."
legal.action: Enforce the signals at fetch time in the acquisition stage.
legal.source: §14.3 item 2; restated in the §17 ACQUISITION block ("robots.txt + noai + TDM-reservation honoured at fetch time")

legal.title: Posture 3 — publish a data statement
legal.detail: Publish a data statement covering sources, licences, filtering, and an opt-out mechanism. Dolma and Common Corpus are the models to copy. "Transparency is a legal asset, not a liability."
legal.action: Publish the data statement alongside the model.
legal.source: §14.3 item 3

legal.title: Posture 4 — run and document memorisation testing
legal.detail: Run and document memorisation testing. The ANI ruling turned on ANI's failure to prove memorisation, so being able to affirmatively demonstrate low memorisation "is now a defensive asset with judicial backing".
legal.status: recommended — now an affirmative legal asset in India
legal.action: Run memorisation tests and publish the results.
legal.source: §14.3 item 4; repeated as the §18.2 mitigation for "Model memorises and regurgitates Indic news"

legal.title: Posture 5 — maintain a takedown/opt-out channel and act on it
legal.detail: Maintain a takedown/opt-out channel and act on it.
legal.action: Stand up the channel and process requests.
legal.source: §14.3 item 5
legal.note: The document gives no SLA for this channel; the only stated deadline is the 90-day DPDP erasure window in L15.

legal.title: Posture 6 — get NCERT/MoE and BharatGen licences in writing
legal.detail: Get NCERT/MoE and BharatGen licences in writing. "Two letters could be worth more than a trillion scraped tokens."
legal.action: Pursue written licences from NCERT/MoE and BharatGen.
legal.source: §14.3 item 6
legal.note: §13.2 adds the specific asks: an MoU for Bharat Data Sagar, and the exact EKA licence string in writing.

legal.title: Keep the clean tier separable against an appeal reversal
legal.detail: Mitigation for the risk "ANI ruling reversed on appeal": keep the clean tier separable so you can retrain a compliant base if needed. "Do not architect a corpus you cannot decompose."
legal.action: Keep the corpus decomposable by licence/risk tier so a compliant base can be retrained.
legal.source: §18.2 Legal and reputational risks

legal.title: Hard-fail the build on any NonCommercial licence tag
legal.detail: Mitigation for "NC-licensed content leaks into the mix": automated licence-tag propagation, and hard-fail the build on any NC tag, not a warning.
legal.action: Propagate licence tags through the pipeline and fail the build (not warn) on any NC tag.
legal.source: §18.2 Legal and reputational risks
legal.note: §18.2 adds a related supply-chain rule for synthetic data: prefer Apache-2.0 generators (Qwen3, some Nemotron) for anything that will be redistributed, to avoid Gemma/Llama/Qwen licence-chain terms.

legal.title: NonCommercial-licensed datasets — exclude from a commercial model
legal.detail: Named NC datasets: NCERT textbooks / DIKSHA textbook content (CC BY-NC-ND, NCERT/MoE, K-12 curriculum in 36 languages — NC and ND); DIKSHA non-textbook resources (CC BY-NC-SA); NPTEL / SWAYAM course content (typically CC BY-NC-SA, MoE/IITs/IISc, 2,500+ courses); AI4Bharat IndicNLP Corpus v1 (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, 2.7B words, 10 languages — IndicCorp v2 and Sangraha are NOT NC, only v1 is); NLLB mined bitext (CC BY-NC, Meta); ILDC Indian Legal Documents Corpus (research/non-commercial by request, Malik et al., 35K SC cases); xLAM some releases (CC BY-NC, Salesforce).
legal.status: in force — exclusion or licence required
legal.action: Exclude from a commercial model unless licensed; verify the specific xLAM release before use.
legal.source: §13.1 ("Everything in this section requires either a licence, a legal sign-off, or exclusion")
legal.note: §A.7 confirms NCERT CC BY-NC-ND and DIKSHA CC BY-NC-SA from NCERT/CIET's own site (high confidence). L10 explains why the ANI ruling does not help here.

legal.title: BharatGen non-commercial model licence blocks distillation
legal.detail: BharatGen Param-2 / Patram post-trained checkpoints carry a BharatGen non-commercial licence. These are models, not data — but the licence blocks distillation-based data generation.
legal.action: Do not generate training data by distilling BharatGen checkpoints without a licence.

legal.title: Bespoke / custom licences requiring negotiation
legal.detail: BhashaKritika, 540B synthetic Indic tokens, Krutrim Community License (Krutrim AI Labs / Ola) — negotiate or replicate. Chitrakshara-IL / Chitrakshara-Cap, Krutrim licence — the largest Indic interleaved multimodal corpus. Bharat Data Sagar (BharatGen consortium) — not distributed; pursue an MoU; ₹1,293 crore of public investment, ~20T tokens claimed.
legal.action: Negotiate, replicate, or pursue an MoU before planning around any of these.
legal.note: §18.3 flags the 20T Bharat Data Sagar figure as unaudited; §A.7 grades it low confidence — "a CEO statement... Do not build a plan that depends on this being true."

legal.title: The Stack v2 — OpenRAIL-M, per-file licences, and a live opt-out list
legal.detail: The Stack v2 / StarCoder2 (BigCode / Software Heritage) is under BigCode OpenRAIL-M v1 plus per-file licences plus a live opt-out list.
legal.action: Ingest the opt-out list and use the permissive-only subset.
legal.note: The opt-out list is live, so it must be re-ingested, not snapshotted once — the document says "ingest the opt-out list" without stating a refresh cadence.

legal.title: AIKosh — per-dataset licence ingestion required
legal.detail: AIKosh datasets carry per-dataset licences: open, registered, or restricted, from various contributors via IndiaAI.
legal.action: Ingest and enforce the licence per dataset rather than treating AIKosh as one licence.

legal.title: ULCA / Bhashini — record-level attribution
legal.detail: ULCA / Bhashini datasets are licensed per contributor with record-level attribution (Bhashini DIBD, MeitY).
legal.action: Maintain an attribution manifest at record level.

legal.title: EKA Pre-training Indic Corpus v1 — licence string unspecified
legal.detail: The EKA Pre-training Indic Corpus v1 (Soket AI Labs + IIT Gandhinagar) is described only as "Open Source" — the licence string is unspecified.
legal.action: Get the exact licence in writing before ingesting.
legal.source: §13.2; repeated in §18.3 Honest unknowns ("EKA corpus licence string is unspecified. Get it in writing.")

legal.title: Share-alike (copyleft) sources — attribution plus share-alike
legal.detail: Wikipedia / Wikisource / Wikibooks / FineWiki (CC BY-SA), FLORES-200 (CC BY-SA 4.0) and People's Speech (CC BY-SA) are usable but carry attribution and share-alike obligations.
legal.action: Attribute, and document your share-alike position.

legal.title: Whether model weights are a derivative work of CC BY-SA data is unresolved
legal.detail: Whether model weights are a "derivative work" of CC BY-SA training data is legally unresolved. "Most labs proceed; document your position."
legal.action: Take and document an explicit position rather than leaving it implicit.
legal.source: §13.3; §18.3 Honest unknowns ("unresolved anywhere in the world")

legal.title: Stack Exchange / Stack Overflow — free bulk use is contested
legal.detail: Stack Exchange / Stack Overflow dumps are CC BY-SA, but Stack Overflow now licenses data commercially to AI firms, so free bulk use is contested.
legal.note: The document says "contested" without stating who is asserting what, or whether the CC BY-SA dump licence has actually been withdrawn.

legal.title: Common Crawl carries third-party copyrighted content
legal.detail: Common Crawl WET/WARC is distributed under CC BY (Common Crawl's own terms) but contains third-party copyrighted content. "The fair-dealing question in §14 lives here."
legal.status: in force — the exposure the ANI ruling addresses
legal.note: This is the direct link between the §13 corpus list and the §14 fair-dealing analysis: the CC licence covers the packaging, not the underlying pages.

legal.title: Absolute blocklist — pirated and litigation-tainted book corpora
legal.detail: Books3: pirated books via the Bibliotek torrent, core to Kadrey v. Meta; the original Pile download URL has been dead since ~Sept 2023. LibGen / Library Genesis: pirated, central to Tremblay v. OpenAI allegations. Anna's Archive / Z-Library: pirated shadow libraries.
legal.action: Never ingest these; if you ingest The Pile, strip Books3 first.
legal.source: §13.4 (cases named: Kadrey v. Meta; Tremblay v. OpenAI)
legal.note: The document names these two US cases only as context for why the datasets are tainted; it states no holding, court, or date for either.

legal.title: LAION-5B — CSAM; use Re-LAION-5B only
legal.detail: CSAM was found in the original LAION-5B dataset (Thiel, Dec 2023) and it was taken down from hosting services; documented PII/medical-record leakage as well.
legal.action: Use Re-LAION-5B (Aug 2024) only, and even then with a fresh safety scan; run PhotoDNA-equivalent hash matching on every image.
legal.source: §13.4 (Thiel, Dec 2023); CSAM hash-matching mitigation in §18.2 and §17
legal.note: Regime left null: the document grounds this in child-safety plus documented PII leakage rather than a named statute.

legal.title: DataComp CommonPool — documented large-scale privacy problems
legal.detail: DataComp CommonPool has documented large-scale privacy problems (arXiv:2506.17185) and substantial overlap with LAION-5B.
legal.action: Avoid, or apply your own PII/CSAM filtering pipeline first.

legal.title: WebVid-10M — withdrawn by its creators
legal.detail: WebVid-10M was withdrawn by its creators.
legal.action: Do not use.
legal.note: The document does not state the reason for the withdrawal.

legal.title: OpenSubtitles — copyrighted film/TV subtitles inside OPUS
legal.detail: OpenSubtitles, distributed within OPUS, is copyrighted film/TV subtitle text.
legal.action: Filter it explicitly out of any OPUS ingestion.
legal.source: §13.4; also flagged in the §7 OPUS row
legal.note: Note the tension the document itself surfaces: §A.4's conversational IndicTrans2 adaptation (arXiv:2606.29024) achieves its result using OpenSubtitles among its "only public data".

legal.title: Alpaca-lineage data — OpenAI ToS provenance taint
legal.detail: Alpaca, Bactrian-X, mAlpaca and many "self-instruct" sets were generated with OpenAI models, and OpenAI's ToS prohibits using outputs to train competing models. "Materially risky for a model that will compete with OpenAI."
legal.action: Prefer Aya, Tülu 3, Nemotron, OpenThoughts, UPDESH instead.
legal.source: §13.4; cross-referenced at §11.1 (Bactrian-X)

legal.title: Reddit / Pushshift — licence or skip
legal.detail: Reddit now licenses data commercially (~$203M disclosed contract value at IPO; ~$60M/yr Google, ~$70M/yr OpenAI reported). Free bulk scraping is against ToS and actively enforced.
legal.action: Do not scrape. License or skip.
legal.source: §13.4; deal figures repeated in §15.2 (all figures "reported", not confirmed by parties)

legal.title: Twitter/X archives — ToS and active enforcement
legal.detail: Twitter/X archives are covered by ToS restrictions with active enforcement.
legal.action: Skip.

legal.title: YouTube-derived corpora — ToS prohibits bulk download
legal.detail: YouTube-Commons, YODAS, Panda-70M, InternVid and HD-VILA are YouTube-derived; YouTube ToS prohibits bulk download regardless of the underlying CC licence on individual videos.
legal.action: Document a position or skip.
legal.source: §13.4; also flagged in §9.2

legal.title: Scraped Indian news — where the risk concentrates
legal.detail: "The ANI v. OpenAI litigation exists precisely because of this." The Digital News Publishers Association and the Federation of Indian Publishers are intervenors. The legal position improved dramatically in July 2026, "but this is where the risk concentrates".
legal.action: For Indian news, negotiate a retrieval/grounding deal rather than a training deal — cheaper, more readily accepted by publishers, and for a conversational model it delivers most of the value.

cleaning_rules.note: Extracted from docs/DECISIONS.md §2 and the pipeline diagram at docs/ATLAS.md §17. The tool register (records/tools.json) covers seven pipeline steps; this covers nine, and the two it adds — the safety gate and synthesis — had no surface anywhere.

stages.name: Acquisition
stages.plain: Fetch it, and be allowed to
stages.does: CC crawls, HF datasets, AIKosh/ULCA, eCourts, PIB, licensed publisher feeds, speech corpora, PDF and print scans.
stages.rule: robots.txt, noai and TDM-reservation honoured at fetch time — not retrospectively.

stages.name: Extraction
stages.plain: Get the words off the page
stages.does: HTML to text (trafilatura, resiliparse), PDF and scans through OCR, speech through ASR, image-text interleaving.
stages.rule: Everyone assumes this is solved. It is solved for English layout.

stages.name: Language and script identification
stages.plain: Work out what language it is in
stages.does: GlotLID script-aware ensemble across all twelve script blocks plus Latin, with code-mix and romanisation detection.
stages.rule: Hinglish is a first-class language here, not noise. Misrouting is invisible — a document sent to the wrong pipeline is simply never seen again.

stages.name: Quality filtering
stages.does: Per-language heuristics, KenLM perplexity against a verified reference, a model-based classifier trained per language, repetition and length checks.
stages.rule: The classifier is the adversary here, not the tool. See the objective-specific rules below.

stages.name: Safety and compliance gate
stages.plain: Remove what must never be trained on
stages.does: PII redaction with Aadhaar, PAN, passport and bank pattern detection; CSAM hash matching on all image data; multilingual toxicity classification; children's-data exclusion; licence-tag propagation; a provenance record carrying URL, licence, hash and retrieval date.
stages.rule: No tool in the register covers this stage. It is the one stage where a miss is not a quality problem but a legal and ethical one — and it is the only stage that has to be built rather than adopted.

stages.name: Deduplication
stages.does: Exact SHA, then global MinHash and LSH across corpora, then embedding-based SemDeDup on the top-quality tier.
stages.rule: This is the step that determines your real token count. Everything quoted before it is a claim about file size.

stages.name: Benchmark decontamination
stages.plain: Make sure the exam is not in the textbook
stages.does: 13-gram overlap plus MinHash against the benchmark blocklist. Every drop logged with the benchmark it matched.
stages.rule: A build gate, not a check — see how we would know it worked.

stages.name: Synthesis
stages.plain: Make more text when there is not enough
stages.does: Translation, transliteration, rephrasing, curriculum generation across 22 languages and five difficulty tiers, document-grounded and persona-grounded generation.
stages.rule: Synthetic text re-enters the quality, dedup and decontamination gates. It is not exempt because you made it.

stages.name: Mixing and tokenisation
stages.plain: Decide the proportions and cut it into tokens
stages.does: Custom tokenizer, temperature-sampled multilingual mixture, phase-scheduled curriculum.
stages.rule: The last stage in the pipeline and the first decision you cannot reverse.

universal.order: NFC and homoglyph normalisation, script-aware language ID, India-specific PII, global MinHash and SemDeDup, 13-gram benchmark decontamination, provenance record

objective_rules.rule: Quality classifiers are the adversary. Per-language calibrated thresholds, never a global one. Tier-3 languages bypass filtering entirely into the protected lane.
objective_rules.counterintuitive: The fix is not a better classifier. It is refusing to let the classifier vote.

objective_rules.rule: Do not length-filter like prose. Licence allowlist plus a live opt-out list. Function-level near-dedup.
objective_rules.counterintuitive: Prose heuristics delete correct code for being terse.

objective_rules.rule: Filter suboptimal trajectories hard. Errors amplify over long horizons — a mediocre 80-turn trace is worse than none.
objective_rules.counterintuitive: This inverts "more data is better". It is the only tier where deleting data reliably improves the model.

objective_rules.rule: Preserve LaTeX. Do not normalise digits.
objective_rules.counterintuitive: Standard text cleaning destroys the notation that carries the meaning.

objective_rules.rule: Temporal validity. Law changes — date-stamp everything.
objective_rules.counterintuitive: Undated statute trains as current fact, and stays wrong for the life of the model.

objective_rules.rule: Build on Qwen3-VL-8B, not olmOCR. Validate on real scans only. Report median and catastrophic-rate, never mean.
objective_rules.counterintuitive: A mean hides the failure mode that matters: rare, total, unrecoverable garbling.

zero_trust.rule: Every dataset passes the full pipeline, including the ones labelled verified.
zero_trust.why: A label is a claim its publisher made, not a measurement you performed. The clearest case in this catalogue is Sangraha, which is the best-documented Indic corpus anybody has built and still ships 251B tokens of which 64B are verified human-origin: roughly 90B is machine-translated from Wikimedia and 72B is romanised transliteration. Nothing is wrong with that — the publisher says so plainly — but a plan that budgets the headline has silently counted machine translation as human text.
zero_trust.consequence: Trust is not transitive and it does not survive a merge. Once corpora are combined, cleaned, shuffled and sharded, a per-document record of what was verified and what was manufactured cannot be reconstructed — so it has to be carried from the first fetch or it does not exist.

growth.note: The lineage runs 3B to 200B in four stages. The 40B the assignment names is stage three, not the start: it is grown from a trained 8B, which was grown from a trained 3B. The method is the four-stage state-preserving growth of arXiv:2606.07404, this project's own prior work, which grew one lineage from a small dense seed through 5B and 9B mixtures of experts to a 120B model. Sizes below are the plan; the corpus figures are what this project is responsible for, and the 40B's is the only one derived rather than proposed.

method.source: arXiv:2606.07404, Reversible Foundations: Training a 120B Sparse MoE through State-Preserving Scaling
method.principle: Each larger model is grown from the trained weights of the smaller one rather than trained afresh.

axes.what: One feed-forward block becomes many, and a router learns to send each token to a few of them.
axes.why_it_matters_for_data: Capacity rises without a matching rise in compute per token, so the corpus does not have to grow in step with the parameter count.

axes.what: Layers are added to a trained stack rather than a deeper stack being trained from scratch.
axes.why_it_matters_for_data: The tokens already read are inherited. Depth added late does not re-read the corpus, which is why the seed's data quality outlives the seed.

axes.what: The expert count rises — in the reported lineage, to 460 under top-12 routing.
axes.why_it_matters_for_data: More experts specialise only if the mixture gives them something to specialise on. A corpus that is 90% English web text produces experts that all learn English web text.

method.warning: The paper reports that several of the failures from getting an expansion wrong are silent — the model trains, the loss falls, and the capability is simply absent. That is the same failure mode this project's five data invariants exist to catch, one level down the stack.

stages.asks_of_the_corpus: Everything, and it is the only stage this catalogue can actually supply. 3T asks for 60B unique tokens of natural Indian-language text and 84.9B can be committed today. Every token read here is inherited by all three stages above, so this is where provenance, licensing and decontamination have to be right rather than fixed later — and the one stage where getting it right is affordable.

basis.why_not_derived: A tokens-per-parameter rule is the one move this page argues against everywhere else: Llama 3.1 trained 8B, 70B and 405B on about the same 15T, so corpus size does not follow parameter count. basis.how: Gemma 4 31B is the model this whole plan is written against, and it publishes no token count — not in its technical report, not on its model card. Its previous generation does: Gemma 3's card states 14T for the 27B (12T for the 12B, 4T for the 4B, 2T for the 1B). 16.8T is that 14T plus 20% for one generation.
basis.checks: Two independent checks. At 420 tokens per parameter for a dense 40B it sits inside the 400-1,900 band every comparable dense model of the last two years occupies. And Chinchilla's compute-optimal ratio of about 20:1 would say 800B, which nobody has planned by in years, because compute-optimal minimises the cost of training while every deployed model pays the cost of serving forever.
basis.assumption: The 20% is an assumption, not a measurement. It is the one free parameter in the derivation, and halving or doubling it moves the budget to 15.4T or 19.6T.

comparators.why_this_one: the predecessor of the model this plan is written against

stages.name: Frontier parity
stages.corpus_basis: Frontier scale: Llama 4 trained on over 30T and Qwen3 on 36T across 119 languages. 30T is parity, not ambition.
stages.asks_of_the_corpus: 600B unique natural Indian tokens — seven times what exists in the catalogue — and the step where the architecture changes. Going sparse buys capacity at roughly a tenth of the compute per token, which is what makes 200B affordable at all; it does nothing whatever for the Indian-language supply.

config.web_data: full corpus, plus the hardest subsets

basis.how: Llama 4 trained on over 30T and Qwen3 on 36T across 119 languages. 30T is parity with figures somebody else published, not a derivation from this plan.
basis.why_not_derived: It is anchored to real published numbers, which makes it the strongest of the three underived stages, but it answers 'what does frontier scale look like' rather than 'what does this model need'. It is also the project's stated aspiration, so it is a target the plan is aiming at rather than a conclusion the plan reached.

acquisition_strategy.rule: Create or partner. Do not purchase.
acquisition_strategy.detail: The corpus is assembled from open sources, from data this project generates itself, and from partnerships and grants — not from bought licences. That is a constraint on the plan rather than a preference, and it changes which blocked datasets are worth pursuing: a letter to a ministry and a data-sharing MoU are in scope, and a commercial publisher licence is not.
acquisition_strategy.consequence: It also raises the value of the three zero-cost items in the acquisition register above everything else in it, and makes the licence questions in the catalogue the highest-leverage unresolved work in the whole project — because an answered licence costs nothing and a bought one is off the table.

invariant.claim: The natural Indian-language pool is a fixed quantity. Holding its share constant means needing more of it at every stage, and there is no more of it.
invariant.detail: The mixture reserves 8% of every batch for natural Indian-language text, read four times. At the 3B seed that asks for 60B unique tokens; at 8B, 160B; at 40B, 336B; at 200B, 600B. What this catalogue can commit is 84.9B of verified human-origin text. It covers the first stage and nothing above it.
invariant.consequence: Every stage of growth makes the Indic tier harder to fill, not easier. The only remedies are collection and partnership, and both are decisions taken years before the model trains.

gap.note: Measured against the seed. This is the finding the exercise exists to produce, and it is the opposite of what most readers expect.
gap.surprise: Every tier is short, and the two that are shortest are the ones nobody expects. Natural Indian text is covered at 25% once machine translation is excluded from the count. Indian civilizational literature is covered at 0% because not one of the 145 catalogued datasets supplies it. What is missing elsewhere — general web, code, maths — is abundant and blocked on a licence nobody has established.
gap.reading: A reader arrives assuming an India-first corpus fails on Indian data. It does not. It fails on the ordinary bulk that everybody assumes is free, and it fails for legal reasons rather than technical ones.

indic_supply.note: The Indic supply route the action chapter kept missing. Every dataset here is already open — its licence permits commercial use — and every one is blocked on work nobody has done rather than on anyone's permission. That distinction is why they never appeared in a queue built around letters.
indic_supply.source: docs/ATLAS.md sections on speech and the week 4-8 plan

asr_route.claim: ASR transcription is one of the only ways to manufacture genuinely natural Indic text at scale.
asr_route.why: India is an oral-first information economy: enormous amounts of Indic language were never written down, so they cannot be crawled. Transcription is the only way to reach them.

hours.source: correction X04 — BhasaAnuvaad (~44,400h, CC BY 4.0) plus IndicVoices, Vaani, SPRING-INX, Shrutilipi, Kathbath, SYSPIN and Rasa; "well north of 100,000 hours". Stated as a floor, not a total: nobody has added the pool up.

words_yield.source: at least 100,000 hours at roughly 9,000 words/hour

asr_route.caveat: Small in raw token terms and extraordinary in distributional value: it is the conversational register web text completely lacks, and conversation is this model's stated primary task. No token figure is given here on purpose — the Atlas counts words, the conversion depends on a tokenizer nobody has trained, and counting it is the first task rather than an assumption.
asr_route.superseded: This chapter planned against 35,000 hours and ~300M words while correction X04, rendered in this page's own appendix, put the open pool well north of 100,000 — an understatement of roughly threefold, in the direction that made the highest-value Indic route look smaller than it is. Both numbers were on one page. The figures here now follow the correction.

rephrasing_route.claim: Rephrasing the committable Indic pool is the cheapest real improvement available to the scarcest tier, and it does not close the gap.
rephrasing_route.how: Restate each collected document several ways with an Apache-2.0 generator, verifying each against its source, then read the enlarged pool fewer times. This is the recipe Kimi K2 published and Kimi K3 still uses; K3's pre-training section does not use the word 'epoch' at all.

evidence.source: Kimi K2 (arXiv:2507.20534) ran the comparison at equal seen tokens: ten epochs over raw data scored about 23.8%, ten rephrasings read once about 28.9% — a 21% relative improvement. One benchmark average, one model, not our languages.

pool_after.source: the 84.9B committable natural-Indic pool, restated twice

worth_gain.source: Muennighoff Eq. 18 applied to the enlarged pool: 170B read 7.9 times is worth about 1,116B against 893B for reading 84.9B 15.8 times, at identical seen tokens

rephrasing_route.cost_note: Shown as a band rather than a figure. The arithmetic is stated so anybody can compute it: tokens generated divided by generation throughput. The throughput is the part nobody here has measured — decode is bound by weight reads rather than FLOPs, so the training-run figure of 4.0e14 FLOP/s does not apply and a plausible range spans an order of magnitude. Across that whole range, doubling the pool once costs well under 1% of the run it feeds, which is why the band is worth reporting and the point estimate is not.
limits: Kimi K2 rephrases each corpus at most twice in production; their ablation went to ten. The sixteen variants it would take to fill this tier with unique text is past anything anybody has reported doing.

Whether a rephrasing counts as a distinct document for the repetition curve has never been measured. The gain above assumes it does. If variants decay faster than fresh text, the gain is smaller than stated and nothing published says by how much.
At two variants — the only depth with production precedent — the tier is still 13% filled by unique text and 87% by repetition. This is an improvement to the slice, not a solution to the shortage.
rephrasing_route.conclusion: It is cheap, it measurably helps, and it leaves the Indic gap where it was. That makes it worth doing and makes it the strongest available argument for funding collection: it is the argument that survives having tried the alternative.

shape.note: What actually grows, across the lineage, and what does not.
shape.finding: Parameters rise sixty-seven fold and the corpus tenfold, while the natural Indian-language text anybody can commit does not move at all. The 3B seed is the only stage its supply covers; by the 40B it is four times short and by 200B seven. Growth does not dilute the Indic share on the chart — the mixture reserves 8% at every stage — it makes that 8% progressively impossible to fill.

growth.config_note:
What a data plan actually decides, stage by stage. Parameter counts belong to whoever designs the architecture; sequence length, what data is admitted and when the quarantine lifts are the corpus team's decisions, and they are the ones that change what has to be collected.

Every stage runs its own complete learning-rate cycle rather than one schedule across the lineage, because each stage is a larger model than the last and reaches a different loss.

Sequence length holds at 8,192 from stage two on. Extending context is an annealing phase after pre-training rather than a stage of it, and no figure for it is proposed here because nothing in this project has measured what it would cost.

quarantine.rule: Script quarantine is absolute at the seed and enforced everywhere above it.
quarantine.what: No code-mixed or romanised Indic text in pre-training. Hinglish and Tanglish enter at instruction tuning, not before.
quarantine.why: A recurrence model accumulates state across a sequence, so a stray Latin token inside a Brahmic one corrupts the state for everything after it. On this architecture mixed script is a structural fault rather than a quality preference — which is a claim from the reference design and is recorded as one, not as a measurement.
quarantine.consequence: It is also the rule that makes the seed stage so hard to fill: the cleanest Indic text is the scarcest, and quarantine removes the code-mixed material that would otherwise pad it.

derivation.question: Why is 16.8T derived and the other three are not?
derivation.method: The derivation anchors to a model, not to a size. This plan is written against exactly one comparator — Gemma 4 31B — and the method is: take the token count that comparator's immediate predecessor published, and add one generation's uplift.
derivation.why_it_does_not_generalise: It needs a named comparator at that stage, and only one stage has one. Nobody publishes the corpus size for an intermediate stage of a lineage they grew — a lab reports the model it shipped, not the 3B it grew that model from. So the other three stages can only be anchored to some other lab's model that happens to be a similar size, and this chapter's own central finding is how weak that substitute is: a corpus is not sized by the model that reads it. Llama 3.1 trained 8B, 70B and 405B on about the same 15T; DeepSeek-V3 stores 671B and read 14.8T, less than Gemma 3's 27B did.
derivation.what_would_fix_it: Two things would turn the other three into derivations. Either a comparator publishes a staged corpus schedule for a grown lineage, which none has; or these stages get sized by supply instead of by analogy — what the catalogue can commit, what licences would unlock, and what the Indic pool is worth at its repetition ceiling are all measured on this page already. The second is available now and is the honest next move.

analogy_note.what_an_analogy_is: Every budget on this ladder except the 40B is set by looking at what some other lab read at a similar parameter count and picking a number near it. That is an analogy, and it is worth stating exactly how much it proves: nothing about this corpus. It carries the assumption that corpus size follows parameter count, which is the assumption this chapter disproves three paragraphs later — Llama 3.1 read about the same 15T for 8B, 70B and 405B, and DeepSeek-V3 stores 671B and read 14.8T, less than Gemma 3's 27B did. The comparators are real published figures. What is invented is the idea that they transfer.
analogy_note.why_keep_them: Because the alternative is a blank. An analogy that is labelled is a placeholder somebody can argue with; a number with no stated origin is one nobody can. They stay, named, until supply can replace them.
analogy_note.what_supply_says_instead: Supply is the other half of the answer and it is the half that is measured here. For any stage the catalogue can be asked two questions with real answers: how much text clears every bar today, and how much more is blocked on nothing but an unanswered licence. Those two numbers do not care what Google read, and unlike the analogies they are properties of this project. Where they fall short of a stage's budget, that gap is the plan's actual content — and at the seed, which admits no web text at all, they fall short by a factor of thirty-five.

scaling_reference.note: What comparable models were actually trained on. Gathered by web research in August 2026 rather than extracted from docs/ATLAS.md, because the Atlas carries only the Indian models and two frontier figures — and the question this record answers (how big a corpus does a 40B seed need, and how does it grow) cannot be settled from five rows. Every entry names the source it was read from. Where a figure is undisclosed it is recorded as null rather than estimated: Gemma 4's token budget is the assignment's own comparator and its technical report does not state it, which is itself the finding.

models.tokens_note: Not disclosed. The technical report's data section (2.4) states only the domains — web documents, code, images, audio — and a January 2025 cutoff. Table 1 gives 29,290M LLM parameters, which is the non-embedding count; the 30.7B here is the total the assignment brief names, and the 262,144 x 6,144 embedding table accounts for the difference.
models.source: arXiv:2607.02770, Gemma 4 technical report, Table 1 and section 2.4
models.why_here: The assignment's named comparator. That its budget is undisclosed is why this project cannot simply match it and has to derive its own.

models.tokens_note: Not disclosed, as with every Gemma 4 variant.
models.why_here: The same family shipping a dense model and a sparse one side by side. 3.8B active of 26B stored is 14.6% — the clearest in-family evidence that the dense-to-MoE move buys capacity without buying proportional compute.
The previous generation of the comparator, and the only Gemma whose budget is public. Its family scales the corpus with the model: 1B on 2T, 4B on 4T, 12B on 12T, 27B on 14T.
The lower rung of the same ladder, showing the family's scaling is roughly one trillion tokens per billion parameters at this size.

models.source: Meta, Llama 3.1 release and the Llama 3 Herd of Models report
models.why_here: The counter-example to Gemma's ladder, and the single most useful row here: Llama 3.1 trained 8B, 70B and 405B on about the same 15T. A corpus is not sized by the model that reads it.
1,875 tokens per parameter — the overtrained end of the range, and the reason a small model can be worth serving.
The scale target's shape: 671B stored, 37B active (5.5%), 256 routed experts plus one shared, trained on 14.8T for 2.664M H800-hours. A 671B model reading no more text than a 27B Gemma.

models.source: Sarvam AI, 'Open-Sourcing Sarvam 30B and 105B' (sarvam.ai/blogs/sarvam-30b-105b): 32B total, ~2.4B active, 128 experts, GQA, 65K context, 16T tokens
models.why_here: The closest Indian peer to the seed size, and it read more text than Gemma 3 27B did.

models.source: Sarvam AI, 'Open-Sourcing Sarvam 30B and 105B': 106B total, ~10B active, 128 experts top-8, MLA, 128K context, 12T tokens
models.why_here: The inversion that makes the point: three and a half times the parameters of Sarvam-30B, trained on a quarter less text.

models.tokens_note: Not stated in the abstract. The paper is a systems and experience report; its contribution is the growth method rather than a corpus.
models.source: arXiv:2606.07404, Reversible Foundations: Training a 120B Sparse MoE through State-Preserving Scaling
models.why_here: The growth method this plan copies. Grown in four stages from a small dense seed through 5B and 9B MoE to 120B with 460 routed experts under top-12 routing, each stage grown from the trained weights of the last. Active parameters rise from 1.78B to 5.93B — about 5% of the 118.67B stored — and the whole lineage runs on single eight-GPU nodes.
The most overtrained Indian model on record: 22T tokens into 2.4B active parameters.
The frontier corpus figure, across 119 languages. The ceiling this plan's last rung is aiming at.
The other frontier figure: over 30T. Stated as a floor rather than a measurement.

findings.claim: A corpus is not sized by the model that reads it.
findings.evidence: Llama 3.1 trained 8B, 70B and 405B on about the same 15T. DeepSeek-V3 at 671B total read 14.8T — less than Gemma 3 27B's 14T is above. Sarvam-105B read 12T where the smaller Sarvam-30B read 16T.
findings.consequence: Growing from a 40B seed to the largest Indic model is not a proportional data problem. Parameters can grow tenfold while the corpus grows by half.

findings.claim: Sparsity is what makes the growth affordable, not more text.
findings.evidence: DeepSeek-V3 activates 37B of 671B stored (5.5%); LightningLM 5.93B of 118.67B (5.0%); Gemma 4's own MoE variant 3.8B of 26B (14.6%); Sarvam-105B 10.3B of 105B (9.8%).
findings.consequence: The step from a dense seed to a sparse successor buys capacity at close to constant compute per token, which is why the growth path is dense-to-MoE rather than dense-to-bigger-dense.

findings.claim: Growth can preserve state rather than restart.
findings.evidence: LightningLM grew one lineage in four stages — dense seed, 5B MoE, 9B MoE, 120B — each from the trained weights of the one before, on single eight-GPU nodes.
findings.consequence: The seed is not a throwaway prototype. Every token it reads is inherited by everything grown from it, which is what makes the seed's data quality the highest-leverage decision in the plan.

findings.claim: None of this helps the constraint that actually binds.
findings.evidence: Every model above grew its corpus by adding English, code and multilingual web text. The natural Indian-language pool measured in this project is about 300B tokens and does not grow because a model got larger.
findings.consequence: At every rung of the growth path the Indic share falls unless somebody funds collection. Scaling makes an India-first model less Indian, not more, unless the collection queue is funded alongside the compute.

density.note: Tokens per parameter, on both denominators. For a sparse mixture of experts the meaningful one is active parameters — the count that actually processes each token — and it is the denominator the 40B seed has to be judged on, because the proposed architecture activates about 5B of its 40B.
density.chinchilla_note: Compute-optimal, and obsolete as a planning figure. It minimises the cost of training; every model below deliberately overtrains because the cost that matters is serving.
density.finding: Comparable models train between 400 and 6,667 tokens per active parameter. The two closest Indian peers bracket the range at 1,200 and 6,667. A 40B sparse model with about 5B active, trained on 16.8T, sits at 3,360 per active parameter — inside that bracket, between Sarvam-105B and Sarvam-30B.
density.against_200b: A 200B-token budget on the same 5B active parameters is 40 tokens per active parameter: twice Chinchilla, and between 10x and 167x below every model in this table. Chinchilla is the wrong anchor for a model that will be served rather than benchmarked, which is the argument this project already makes for training past compute-optimal.
